activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: During Diwali, celebrated by Hindus, Jains, Sikhs and some Buddhists, families light small oil lamps called diyas in homes and temples to symbolize light overcoming darkness.
story:
The diyas arrived in crates of straw, forty of them, each a small clay bowl with a cotton wick curled inside like a sleeping question. Eli's mother set him to work on the temple steps while she argued with his aunt about the order of the tables, and the street behind them was already filling with the smell of frying and the clatter of a stage being assembled for the evening's celebration. He filled each bowl with oil, pressed the wick down with one finger, and set it in a row, and the rows stretched from the temple door to the curb, waiting for a light that had not yet been given.

He had told Raphaelle and Winston he would meet them at the festival by seven, and it was already quarter past. They had a plan, or Winston had a plan, which amounted to finding the food stalls first and working outward, and Raphaelle had texted twice, the second text only a question mark. Eli looked at his phone, then at the crates still half full of unlit lamps. His mother wanted the steps finished before the guests arrived at eight, and she had that particular steadiness in her voice that meant the request was not really a request.

Ms. Chatterjee from three doors down appeared at the bottom of the steps with a plate of sweets she was carrying to the temple kitchen. She was not Hindu, and Eli had watched her come to the festival every year anyway, standing at the edge of the crowd with her hands folded, taking it in the way some people take in weather. "You've done this since you were small," she said, watching him pour. "I never asked. Why the little lamps?"

He started to answer and found he had to think about it, which surprised him. He knew the motions the way he knew how to tie his shoes, without being able to say why the loop went around twice. "They're called diyas," he said. "We light them at home and in the temple. Light winning over darkness, that's the whole idea." She nodded slowly, as if filing it somewhere, and carried her plate inside.

His phone buzzed again. Winston: we're at the north end, where are you. Eli stood with the last crate at his feet and let himself ruminate for a moment, which he knew was a mistake, because thinking about a choice was a way of already half making it. There was the version of the evening where he slipped away and found his friends and the food stalls, and the version where he stayed until the guests came, and both of them felt true. His mother had never once said the words family comes first; she had only ever lit the lamps and expected him to follow with the matches.

An old man Eli did not know came up the steps with a box of matches and began moving along the row, touching flame to wick. Where he had passed, the clay bowls caught and held small teardrops of fire, and the oil in each one trembled at the heat. Eli watched a single flame travel the length of the temple wall, one bowl to the next, and understood the design of it for the first time: nobody lit these alone. It was a milieu built out of hundreds of small individual acts, his rows and the old man's matches and his mother's arguments about tables, none of it working unless all of it worked.

He texted Winston: north end, stay there, twenty minutes. Then he crouched and helped the old man light the remaining lamps on the second row, and the man said something in Hindi that Eli half caught, something about doing it properly, and laughed, and Eli laughed too because the man was right, his last three wicks had been pressed in crooked and one of them drowned.

At the bottom of the steps a boy of maybe nine was standing with his hands in his pockets, watching the flames the way Ms. Chatterjee watched the whole festival, from outside. His kurta was clean but thin, and Eli recognized him vaguely from the neighborhood, one of the families the temple committee kept a quiet list of, indigent, his mother had said once, using the word carefully, and then gone to their door with a bag of rice. The boy did not move toward the temple.

Eli looked at his phone, at the time, at the north end of the street where Winston and Raphaelle were presumably eating something Winston had declared the best in the city. Then he took two unlit diyas from the crate, filled them, and set one in front of the boy with the box of matches beside it. "Light overcoming darkness," Eli said. "That's the point. You can hold it while you watch." The boy picked up the matchbox and turned it over in his hands, studying it, and struck one against the side, and the wick caught, and he held the lamp up between them, cupping the flame against the moving air of the street.

"You're missing your friends," the boy said, nodding at Eli's phone.

"They'll keep," Eli said, and sat down on the step beside him, and the lamp burned between them.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: In the United States and Canada, shelf and menu prices usually do not include sales tax, which is added at the register, so the total is higher than the posted price.
story:
The accountant's office smelled of toner and old coffee, and Charles sat with his father's shoebox of receipts on his lap while Mr. Zhao sorted them into fanned little cities across the desk. He had come because his father, laid off in March, had said the return was Charles's job this year, and because Charles, eighteen and about to start college in the fall, had agreed before he understood what agreeing would involve. Mr. Zhao worked without ceremony, sliding a receipt for eighty-one dollars of truck parts under a paperclip and murmuring that it might be deductible, that deductions reduced the income the tax was calculated on, that some of these would survive scrutiny and some would not. Charles had brought a notebook and was trying to transcribe everything, his pen moving in small obedient strokes.

His friend Meliane sat in the corner chair by the window, waiting for her own appointment. She wanted the education credit sorted before the tuition deadline, and she had said on the bus that if she didn't get it, she would take a second shift at the garden centre and simply not sleep in September. She had the stillness of someone conserving herself. When Mr. Zhao asked whether her employer had withheld anything from her summer pay, she produced a final pay stub, and Charles leaned over despite himself. The gross pay at the top and the net pay at the bottom were different numbers, and between them sat a column of withholdings, income tax among them, small and regular as fence posts. He had never looked at his own stubs this closely. Money left before it ever reached you; that was the part that unsettled him, the way the cheque was already an aftermath.

At noon Mr. Zhao's receptionist went to lunch, and Charles volunteered for the food run, mostly to escape the fanned cities of receipts and the sense that his father's year was being audited like a character. Meliane came with him because the deli was two doors down and because, she said, if she sat still any longer she would start doing arithmetic about her life. She had done that arithmetic already; he could see it in her shoulders.

At the counter he ordered the turkey sandwich, which was posted at nine dollars, and a coffee for Mr. Zhao and a soup for Meliane, and he counted his crumpled bills on the little ledge: fourteen dollars exactly, which he had calculated on the walk over against the posted prices, adding nothing because nothing needed adding, he thought. The cashier rang it up and the screen said fifteen and change. Charles stood there.

"I have fourteen," he said. "The prices add up to fourteen."

"Sales tax," the cashier said, not unkindly, already reaching to remove the coffee.

And Charles understood, in one somatic flash of heat along his neck, that the menu prices had never included the tax; that in the United States and Canada, shelf and menu prices usually did not include sales tax, which was added at the register, so the total came out higher than the posted price. He had done the arithmetic correctly and still arrived in the wrong place. He had been paying tax on things for years, of course, but somehow he had never once watched it happen; it had always been his father's card, his mother's card, a blur at the register.

Meliane slid a two-dollar coin across the ledge before he could speak. "Take the soup out if you have to," she told the cashier, "but take nothing out of the coffee, it's not for us." Then, to Charles, quietly: "I did the same thing my first week at the garden centre. Bought a granola bar with exact change and stood there like a person meeting gravity for the first time."

He carried the bag back one-handed, the other hand holding her coin, which she refused to take back. In the office, Mr. Zhao drank his coffee and looked over Charles's notebook, where the transcribed columns of deductions ran down the page like the withholding column on Meliane's stub, everything subtracted from something larger. Charles said, carefully, that he was trying to decide whether it was fair, the whole arrangement; money removed before you held it, prices that were not the price. Mr. Zhao said that fairness was above his pay grade, that his job was closer to rectitude, which was only the honest arithmetic of what the rules already said. Charles thought that was a dodge, and also that it wasn't, and could not split the difference.

He copied the final numbers onto the return, checked them twice, and signed his father's name where the form allowed the preparer's line, his own beneath it in careful full letters. Meliane was still waiting for her turn, spinning her pay stub on the desk edge. When Mr. Zhao finally waved her forward, Charles stood to go, and she looked up and said, "Come back Thursday and tell me what they owe you. I'll buy the coffee. I know now to bring more than it says."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Pierre de Coubertin designed the five Olympic rings in 1913, choosing colors so that every national flag of the time contained at least one of them, including the white background.
story:
The game didn't start until eight, but by six the living room smelled of her mother's chili and Mr. Paquette had already claimed the good chair, the one with the cup holder. He had come over because his television had died on Tuesday and he refused to miss the final. Khadija sat cross-legged on the floor with a bowl of chips she was not sharing, and Crosby lay across the couch with his shoes on until Alexa's mother looked at him, at which point the shoes came off without a word being spoken.

They were watching the Olympic final, the women's relay, and Alexa's mother had hung a paper flag over the television that morning. It was crooked, and nobody had straightened it, and by six thirty Alexa could not stop noticing it. Her father kept walking past it on his way to refill Mr. Paquette's glass, pausing each time as if the flag were a shrine he was obliged to acknowledge. He had done the same thing four years ago. In Alexa's memory of that summer he had stood in this same room, this same hour of the evening, and told the neighbors that the rings on the screen stood for the five continents, one color each, and that the blue was Europe. The neighbors had nodded. Alexa had been fourteen and had nodded too.

Tonight he did it again. "You know the rings," he said, gesturing at the screen with Mr. Paquette's glass. "Five continents. Blue for Europe." Crosby raised his head from the couch. "That's not right," he said. "I read that's a myth." Her father laughed, not unkindly, the laugh of a man defending furniture he had lived with for years. "A myth. Everything's a myth now. It's all relativism with you people, whatever you believe is true for you."

Khadija put down the chips. "It's not relativism if there's an answer," she said. "Somebody designed them. It's not like a poem." This was the problem with the evening, Alexa understood, and it wasn't really about rings. Her father liked to aggrandize the things he half remembered, and Crosby liked to catch people doing it, and her mother wanted everyone to enjoy the chili, and all three of these wants could not survive in one room unless somebody found the actual answer.

Alexa got her phone. She typed slowly because Khadija was reading over her shoulder and Mr. Paquette was offering commentary from the good chair about how in his day you just believed your father and that worked fine, which made her mother laugh into the pot on the stove. The page loaded. She read it twice.

"It was Pierre de Coubertin," she said. "He designed the rings in 1913." Her father opened his mouth and she kept going, faster. "He picked the colors so that every national flag of the time contained at least one of them. Including the white background." The room went quiet except for the pregame commentary. "So there's no continent for each color. The colors are just the colors that show up in all the flags. Blue is in our flag, it's in Khadija's flag, it's in everybody's flag somewhere." Crosby sat up and pointed at her with a chip, vindicated, and her father stood very still under the crooked paper flag.

"White's a color," said Khadija's little brother, who had been silent for an hour and was only there for the chips. "The background counts." He said it the way you announce a goal.

"I know the background counts," her father said. He looked at the screen, where the rings turned slowly behind the commentators' heads, and then at the paper flag over the television, and then, briefly, at Alexa. "Coubertin," he repeated, as if testing the weight of it. He didn't say he was wrong, exactly, but he refilled Mr. Paquette's glass and sat down on the arm of the couch, which he never did, and when the relay started twenty minutes later he shouted at the television with the rest of them. Between the second and third legs, Crosby, who was nocturnal by instinct and had been wrecked all week by the diurnal schedule of the broadcasts, fell asleep with a chip still in his hand. Khadija took a picture. When the anchor leg came down to the last fifty meters, Alexa's father was on his feet, and so was Mr. Paquette, and the paper flag slid loose on one corner and hung there, still not quite straight, while they all screamed at the screen.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Linguist Merrill Swain's output hypothesis holds that trying to speak or write a language makes learners notice gaps in what they know, which helps them learn.
story:
The topic was drawn on Monday and the debate was on Friday: whether the city should offer amnesty to people who had ridden the transit system without paying for years, an amnesty in exchange for registering and paying a reduced fine. Nathaniel had volunteered for the Spanish section, mostly because Ashwin had dared him to, and now the dare had hardened into a schedule taped inside his locker. Five minutes, no English, in front of Mr. Yoon's fourth-period class.

He prepared the way he always prepared for anything: silently. He read three articles, two in English and one in Spanish, and made a page of notes with the good phrases underlined. His position, as far as he had one, was that amnesty was practical but felt wrong, that forgiving fare evasion because enforcement had been lazy was like forgiving a debt to whoever shouted loudest. He liked the sentence. He could not say how he would translate it, but that seemed like a Friday problem.

Thursday after school he sat in the emptying library with Ashwin and Nathanael, who had both done their debates already and had the loose, unhelpful cheerfulness of survivors. "Test me," Nathaniel said. "Ask me anything."

Ashwin asked, in slow textbook Spanish, whether the policy was fair to people who had always paid. Nathaniel opened his mouth and found nothing in it. He knew the word for fair, he was almost sure, and he knew people, and he knew pay, but between them the sentence would not stand up. He tried a workaround, something like the people who gave money all the time, and heard how clumsy it was, and stopped. "That was ten seconds," Nathanael said, checking his phone. "You've got four minutes fifty left."

Nathaniel put his head in his hands. "I read the articles. I understood them. I have ideas."

"You have ideas in English," Ashwin said. He turned his laptop around. He had been scrolling, half-listening, and had landed on something from a linguistics course page. "Listen to this. Merrill Swain's output hypothesis. Speaking or writing the language makes you notice the gaps in what you know, and that's how you learn. It's called the output hypothesis."

"I don't have time to learn Spanish by Thursday."

"That's not the point. You already know more than you think. You just can't see it until you try to say it out loud. The gaps show up when you talk."

Nathanael slid a stack of blank cards across the table. "So we find the gaps tonight." They spent the next hour in a strange, patient ritual: Ashwin asked questions in Spanish, Nathaniel answered in whatever he had, and every time he stalled, Nathanael wrote the missing word on a card, the Spanish on one side and, underneath, the sentence Nathaniel had wanted to say. Tarifa. Justicia. De hecho, which meant actually and which Nathaniel said five times until it lost its strangeness. The stack grew to fourteen cards, then twenty. Each one was a small embarrassment, and each one, once turned over and said aloud, stopped being one.

What surprised him was not the vocabulary but the argument. Pushed to say the policy was useful, he reached for the sentence about debts and shouting and couldn't build it, and in rebuilding it more simply, something shifted. Fairness was one thing; the city's own records, which he'd underlined in English, showed that enforcement had fallen almost entirely on two subway lines, on students, on people his age. His clever objection about loud debtors belonged, he admitted, to a world where everyone had been equally likely to be caught, and that world was an anachronistic one, a version of the debate from before the numbers existed. He didn't drop the objection entirely. He held both of them, the principle and the record, and couldn't yet say which should win, and that unfinished feeling was, he suspected, more honest than the clean page of notes had been.

Friday came. He stood at the front with his cards face down, having decided he would not look at them. Mr. Yoon started the timer. Nathaniel's first sentence came out too fast and he made himself slow down. Somewhere in the second minute he reached for a word and felt the gap open under him, exactly where Ashwin's questions had opened it the night before, and this time he stepped around it, and the detour turned out to be a better sentence than the one he'd planned. In the last minute a girl in the second row, one who had ridden those lines every day for three years, raised her hand, and the timer ran out with her hand still up and Nathaniel already turning toward her, saying, in Spanish, "Sigue. Please, go on."

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: On a stage in the round, the audience sits on all sides, so the director must keep actors moving so no section only sees their backs.
story:
Laurence had three days to turn twelve pages of blocking into something an audience could watch from every side, and the auditorium, which had promised her a stage, had instead delivered a square of taped floor with chairs pushed around it in a ragged ring.

"It's supposed to be this way," said Eden, dropping into one of the folding chairs with her script. "Ms. Ferreira's class took the actual stage for the dance showcase. We're in the round now. Thrust into the round, actually, which is worse, if that's possible."

"The round," Laurence repeated, as though the word might soften if she said it gently.

"Chairs on all four sides," Eden said. "Congratulations, Director."

Laurence had spent two weeks blocking the one-act as if the audience lived in one place, a single invisible eye at the back wall of the auditorium. She'd built it around a long dinner-table scene, Anna and her brother face to face, which had looked beautiful in her notebook and now, on the taped square, meant that somebody was always staring at the back of somebody's head. She tried it once. Chiara, playing Anna, delivered the play's most wounded line to the north section of chairs, and the south section got a view of Chiara's shoulder blades doing their best.

"Well," said Eden from the chairs, "the south row just experienced that scene as avant-garde mime."

"Be facetious somewhere else," Laurence said, but she was already pacing the square, and a memory had caught up with her. Eighth grade, the community theatre her mother had dragged her to, a production of Our Town where the seats wrapped the actors like a moat. She remembered being furious, thirteen and squirming, because for whole minutes she'd watched a man's back, and then how the man had turned, mid-speech, a slow quarter-rotation like a door on a hinge, and suddenly the scene belonged to her section too. She hadn't known the word for it then. She knew now, or she was starting to: the director couldn't let anyone stand still for long, because with the audience on all sides, some part of it only sees backs. Movement wasn't decoration here. Movement was fairness.

"New rule," she announced. "Nobody parks. You're all planets. You drift."

"I don't drift," said Chiara. "I have a knee."

"You drift sympathetically."

Mr. Tanaka, who had wandered in to collect a crate of extension cords and had clearly decided to stay, lowered himself into a chair with the air of a man at a tennis match. He said nothing, which Laurence suspected was his version of mercy. She appreciated it. The last thing she needed was an adult explaining the metaphysics of theatre in the round to her, as if she hadn't already felt it in her teeth.

The hard part was not the rule but the dinner scene. In her original blocking, Anna sat and the brother stood, a static image of power she'd been quietly proud of. Now the stillness was a flaw, and she had to decide whether to save the image or the scene. She tried having the brother circle the table while Anna stayed seated, and it was terrible, a shark pacing a lagoon. She tried both of them orbiting each other, and Chiara started laughing halfway through because it looked like a folk dance. On the third try, she gave up the table entirely and moved the argument onto the floor, no furniture, the two of them passing through the space like weather, and each quarter of chairs got, in turn, a face, a profile, a gesturing hand. The scene stopped being about who sat above whom. It became about two people who could not hold still around each other. Laurence stood in the middle of the square and felt something click shut, or open, she couldn't have said which.

"It's better," Eden admitted, "which is annoying, because I liked the table. The table was a metaphor."

"The table was furniture. You can sublimate your grief about it into your performance."

"My performance is already all grief. You keep adding grief."

Rehearsal ran until the janitor rattled his keys at the door. Thursday night, Laurence sat alone in the auditorium's last lit row with her notebook, redrawing the whole play in arrows and spirals, trying to make every entrance and turn pay rent to all four sections of chairs. Some of it she was certain of. Some of it, like whether the final monologue should rotate slowly or be delivered in four static pieces, one to each side, she could not settle, and she wrote both options in the margin and boxed neither. She was honest enough with herself, at least, to know that this was not a decision she could make on paper. It was a decision the room would make, or the actors, or the moment, and tomorrow she would have exactly one run-through to find out.

Friday evening, the chairs filled. Her mother came, and Eden's grandfather, and half of Mr. Tanaka's stagecraft class, and they sat on all sides of the taped square like a jury. The lights came up, borrowed and wobbly, and Chiara walked out and did not stand still. She turned through her first speech so that every side of the room got her face in turn, unhurried, as if she were simply a person speaking to everyone at once, and Laurence, kneeling by the light board with her heart going like a drum line, watched the south section lean forward.

"Planets," Eden whispered from the tech table.

"Drift," Laurence whispered back, and pushed the slider up.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Spanish news writers often attribute a claim with 'según', meaning 'according to', which tells a reader the statement comes from a source, not the reporter.
story:
The festival program listed his name in print, which made it worse. "Aidan Reyes, Spanish learner, will read and summarize today's news, 3 p.m., Community Stage." His slot was forty minutes away, and he still could not tell whether the article in his hands said the harbor cleanup had succeeded or merely that someone claimed it had.

Giuliano had found the article for him that morning, torn from a Spanish-language daily and folded into a paper crane, because Giuliano believed all information should arrive decorated. "It's short," Giuliano said now, unfolding it against a table of churros. "Two hundred words. You could memorize it."

"That's not summarizing, that's reciting. I'm not a parrot."

"You're not a parrot," Haley agreed, arriving with two lemonades and the calm of someone whose own festival job was watching a fish tank. She worked the marine conservation booth ten feet away, under a banner about pelagic species, tuna and mackerel drifting across a painted blue that had begun, in the afternoon heat, to peel. "A parrot doesn't get nervous. A parrot just wants a cracker."

He read the article again. Most of it yielded: the port, the volunteers, the mayor, the bags of trash. Then came the sentence that had stopped him at noon and had metastasized in his mind since, spreading from a small grammatic worry into the fear that he would stand on a stage and tell three hundred people something false. "La bahía está limpia, según el director del proyecto." The bay is clean. But según what? Según whom? In his first-year class, according to Mr. Patel, his errors had a way of hiding in exactly the words that looked easiest.

"What does según mean?" he asked Haley, because Giuliano had wandered off to negotiate with the churro man and was therefore useless.

"No idea. Ask your teacher."

"Mr. Patel judges the reading contest at two." Which was now. Which meant Mr. Patel was somewhere on this grass, closer every minute, and would be sitting in the front row when Aidan stood up.

He found Mr. Patel at the judging table, scoring a girl who was reciting a Neruda poem with terrifying confidence. Aidan waited at the edge of the table until the scorecard went down. "I have a word I can't crack. In the article. I don't want to get it wrong on stage."

"Which word?"

"Según."

Mr. Patel smiled in the way that had earned him the nickname the Pedagogue, though never to his face. "Look where it sits. What comes after it?"

"A person. The project director."

"Then it means 'according to.' Spanish news writers use it to say a claim comes from a source, not from the reporter." He turned back to the scorecards. "The reporter isn't telling you the bay is clean. The reporter is telling you that somebody said so."

Aidan stood there a moment while the girl finished Neruda and applause went up like startled birds. So the sentence wasn't a fact at all. It was a report of a claim, and his whole summary had to change shape: not "the bay is clean," but "according to the project director, the bay is clean," which was a smaller and truer thing to say. He thought of Haley's painted tuna, swimming in a blue that was only pretending to be an ocean. Then he thought: this is actually the point of the whole exercise. Somebody states, somebody attributes, somebody decides how much to believe. He could do that on a stage. He could do that anywhere.

He ran the new summary twice under his breath while Giuliano, returned and powdered with sugar, timed him on a phone. Twenty-two seconds. Fifteen. Giuliano kept adjusting one word and Aidan kept rejecting the adjustment, and their argument was still running when the stage manager leaned out from behind the curtain and pointed at him with the program folded in her hand.

Aidan walked up into the lights, unfolded the article, and began. He read the harbor, the volunteers, the bags of trash. Then he paused, looked at Mr. Patel in the front row, and said, "Y según el director del proyecto, la bahía está limpia. According to the project director. Not according to me."

From the back, Haley raised her lemonade. Giuliano cupped his hands around his mouth and shouted, "¡Exactamente, loro!" which meant, roughly, exactly, parrot, and Mr. Patel wrote something down that Aidan could not see.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: The US federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009, though many states and cities set a higher minimum.
story:
James filled out the application at the counter of the coffee shop with a pen that kept skipping, so that his address looked like it had been censored for security reasons. Mr. Addo, the owner, watched him struggle the way a man watches weather. "You start Saturday," he said at last. "Seven twenty-five an hour, plus tips if anyone ever tips in this town."

"Seven twenty-five," James repeated, because it was the first number anyone had ever paid him, and he wanted to hold it up to the light.

Saturday came, and James learned that the espresso machine had moods, that the pastry case could be restacked into a kind of architecture, and that a small coffee in this shop was called a "tall" for reasons no customer understood either. By Tuesday he had a paper check, actual paper, with his name printed in a font that suggested the government. He photographed it and sent it to Raiden, who had just been hired at a chain sandwich place one state over, across the river, twenty minutes by bus.

Raiden's reply arrived at eleven that night: a photo of his own check, and beneath it, "bro why are you making more than me." James squinted at the tiny numbers. Raiden's hourly rate sat above his, plain as a toaster. He texted back, "I'm not making more. I make 7.25." Then he stared at the two images, side by side, like a detective with two photographs of the same suspect.

At school the next morning he found Raiden at the lockers, and they were joined by Austyn, who claimed to know everything about money and generally knew about a third of it. "It's because the state over there is richer," Austyn said. "It's because you got scammed," Raiden said. "It's because the bus company owns the sandwich chain," Austyn added, which even he did not seem to believe. James held up a hand. "I beseech you both to stop talking," he said, and pulled out his phone.

The search took four minutes, and the answer, when it assembled itself, was quieter than any of Austyn's theories. The federal minimum wage had been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009, which meant it had been born when James was three and had never once grown. But, and here was the part that untangled the checks, many states and cities set a higher minimum of their own. Raiden's state was one of them. James's was not. He read the line twice, feeling the strange vertigo of learning that a number he'd taken for the floor of the world was only one floor, and a low one.

"So I'm being paid the least that is legally allowed anywhere in this country," James said, as they walked to class, "and you're being paid the least that is legally allowed over a bridge."

"Basically," said Raiden, who was grinning now. Austyn, refusing defeat, argued that it was still a scam, and James conceded the point generously, since it was also, technically, the law. He turned the idea over through chemistry and lunch. He had liked the number when Mr. Addo said it, felt almost proud of it, and now the same number looked like a small door in a small room. Both feelings were true. He could not make them into one clean feeling, and he decided, with the mild stubbornness of someone newly eighteen, that he did not have to.

On Saturday he came in early and worked the register without complaint, because complaint was not the plan. The plan, hatched on the walk home from school and refined by text with Raiden, was simpler: keep the job, keep the tips, and find out, politely, whether the shop three streets over, the one inside the city limits rather than just outside them, was hiring. At closing, wiping down the tall, short, inexplicably medium-sized machine, he asked Mr. Addo whether he'd ever thought about moving the shop twenty minutes down the road.

Mr. Addo looked up from the register drawer. "Move the whole shop?"

"Just the concept of it," James said. "Maybe the chairs."

Mr. Addo laughed, a sound like gravel being poured into a bucket, and slid a day-old croissant across the counter. "Eat," he said. "Negotiators need their strength."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: New Zealand was the first country to adopt formal inflation targeting, when its government and Reserve Bank agreed in March 1990 on a target range of 0 to 2 percent.
story:
Claire had promised her grandmother she would explain, by Sunday dinner, why raising interest rates slows inflation, and she was beginning to regret the promise. She sat on the bench outside the changing rooms in the mall with her economics textbook open on her knees, watching Katerina flip through a rack of dresses she had no intention of buying. The mall's air conditioning hummed at a pitch that seemed to portend nothing good for anyone's mood, and Claire had read the same paragraph four times without taking anything in.

"You're doing the face," Katerina said, holding a green dress against herself without looking at the mirror. "The one where you're arguing with a book."

"It doesn't make sense to me yet. I can recite it. Higher rates make borrowing expensive, so people spend less, so prices stop climbing. But Gran is going to ask why, and she'll keep asking why until I fall through the floor."

Sterling came out of the changing room in a shirt two sizes too deliberate and posed with his hands on his hips. "Rate hikes cool the economy," he said. "There. Tell her that."

"Cooling isn't an explanation, it's a metaphor," Claire said. "Metaphysics is easier than this."

"That's not what metaphysics means," Katerina said.

"I know what it means. I mean at least in metaphysics nobody pretends you can measure it in percent."

Ms. Aquino, who taught history at the high school and apparently shopped here on Saturdays, appeared at the end of the aisle with a shopping bag and a look of amused recognition. She had overheard enough, she said, to be curious what the three of them were doing with a textbook in a clothing store on a Saturday. When Claire explained the dinner, the promise, the grandmother who read the financial pages and asked questions like a prosecutor, Ms. Aquino sat down on the bench beside her without being invited.

"When I was in Auckland," Ms. Aquino said, "I taught a boy who wrote his whole thesis on this."

"New Zealand?" Claire said.

"His grandfather worked at the Reserve Bank, back at the start of the nineties. He told me something I never forgot." She paused, apparently deciding whether to go on, then did. "New Zealand was the first country to adopt formal inflation targeting. The government and the Reserve Bank agreed in March 1990 on a target range of zero to two percent. Before that, nobody had promised the public a number."

Claire wrote it in the margin of her notebook, twice, because the first time her hand was unsteady. "So there was a first time. Somebody had to decide that a bank should aim at a number and tell everyone the number."

"That's all I know," Ms. Aquino said, standing. "The rest is your dinner problem." She wished them luck and walked off toward the food court, and Sterling said she was the reason he'd liked history class, and Katerina said he had never liked history class.

They ended up at the table by the fountain, the one where the noise of the water made a kind of privacy, and Claire laid the textbook aside and worked through it out loud, using the dresses and the shirt and the bags around them as her props. If borrowing costs more, Katerina's mother delays the new kitchen, and the contractor doesn't raise his prices because nobody's buying. If saving pays better, Sterling's father moves money out of spending and into deposits. The mall itself became the illustration: half the shops had sale signs, the ones whose customers needed credit, and the others, the phone stores, did not. She talked until her voice went flat and Katerina went morose with boredom and Sterling started charging her imaginary tuition, and then she stopped, because a thought had arrived.

"The thing I can't explain," she said, "is why it has to hurt a little before it works. Everyone who loses their job to this did nothing wrong. That part isn't in the book."

"So say that," Katerina said. "Say the part you don't know. Gran likes you better when you're stuck, she told me."

At Sunday dinner Claire passed the potatoes and gave the explanation once, slowly, the borrowing and the spending and the prices, and when her grandmother asked who decided banks should aim at a number, Claire told her about New Zealand, March 1990, the zero to two percent range, the first country to make the promise formal. Her grandmother put down her fork. "I remember when that was in the papers," she said. "I thought it would never last." She asked one more question, about the people in between, and Claire said, honestly, that she didn't have an answer for that yet, and reached for the potatoes again.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: Since 1975, ending most debate in the US Senate through cloture has required three-fifths of senators, which is 60 votes when all 100 seats are filled.
story:
The email arrived at 9:47 on a Tuesday, and Parker read it three times before he let himself believe it. His model Youth Legislature bill, the one he had drafted in November and mailed off with a stamp from the kitchen drawer, had been selected for the state's mock Senate session in April. Selected, not waitlisted. He sat at his desk with the cursor blinking in the search bar and the radiator ticking under the window, and he thought about Ms. Ito from the Youth Legislature office calling it "a real bill for real committees," which had sounded like flattery until now.

His bill would raise the state minimum age for solo night driving from sixteen to seventeen. He had written it in one sitting, forty minutes, confident the logic carried itself: crashes, statistics, insurance tables. But the selection email said bills would face committee review, floor debate, recorded votes, and, if passed by both chambers, the signature of the student governor, whose assent or veto made the whole thing official. Rereading that list, Parker understood how little he had actually thought about any of it. He had thought a bill was an argument. It seemed now that it was more like a rock being carried down a river, worn at every bend.

He opened a new document and titled it PROBLEMS, then typed nothing. Instead he pulled up the contact he had been avoiding, the phone number for Mr. Bear, his old civics teacher, who had moved three doors down last year and now watered his tomatoes in a shirt that said MAGISTRATE in cracked iron-on letters, a souvenir, he claimed, from a mock-trial summer that had gotten out of hand.

Jazmin texted first, which was typical. U got in??? She had submitted a bill about requiring menstrual products in school bathrooms, and hers had been selected too, along with Quinten's, which would ban single-use plastic at school events. They arranged to meet Saturday at Parker's house, three laptops on his bedroom floor like a war council with snacks.

Jazmin arrived early and sat on the bed, cross-legged, arms folded in a way Parker had learned to read as pre-debate. She had already found the committee assignments. His bill was in Transportation, hers in Education, and the chairs were strangers from a private school across the state. "You should find out who they are," she said. "Chairs decide which bills die in committee without ever reaching a floor vote. That's the whole trick. Nobody announces it. The bill just never comes up."

Quinten came in eating a granola bar and talking about the Senate. In April, he said, the organizers were going to stage a realistic Senate day, with real procedural rules, and there was a rumor that the student presiding officer had been given actual parliamentary scripts. He had been researching, because his plastics bill was popular but not unanimous, and he was nervous. "A senator gave a whole speech once about ending debate. There's a word for it. Cloture."

"Ending debate," Parker repeated. He typed it into the search bar and the radiator ticked twice while the page loaded.

There it was, plain as igneous rock laid down in layers: to end most debate in the United States Senate took three-fifths of the senators, which was 60 votes when all 100 seats were filled. He stared at the number. Fifty-five supporters, he thought, was a majority. Fifty-five was more than half of anything. And yet a bill with fifty-five supporters in the Senate could still fail, could still sink with the majority on its side, because fifty-five was not sixty. Jazmin leaned over his shoulder and read the line aloud, and Quinten said quietly, "So you can win the vote and lose the bill," and nobody answered for a second because there was nothing clever to add.

Parker saved the page and then sat back. The three of them spent the afternoon war-gaming the committee hearing, and he discovered, in a way that embarrassed him, that his own bill was the weakest. Quinten, playing the role of hostile committee chair, asked him who had been consulted, and Parker had no answer. Rural kids who needed to drive to jobs at night. Parents who carpooled. He had not historicize d anything; he had treated sixteen as a fixed constant rather than a number a legislature had once chosen and might choose again, for reasons, in a year, with a name attached. He said as much out loud, and Jazmin said, "Then say that at the hearing. Say you talked to the other side. Even if the other side is your uncle."

He spent the following week on the phone with his uncle Dean, who drove a delivery route, and with two juniors from the next town over, and he revised the bill to include a hardship exemption he had sworn on Saturday he would never concede. On Monday he walked down to Mr. Bear's tomatoes with a printed copy.

Mr. Bear read it standing up, one hand on the trellis. He did not lecture. He asked two questions, pointed at a badly worded clause, and then said, "You know the governor can still veto it. Both chambers pass it and one person refuses assent, and then you need two-thirds to override." He handed the pages back. "That's not a flaw in the system. That's the system."

Parker stood there holding his own bill, hearing the whole machinery of it, drafting, committee, debate, cloture waiting like a wall at sixty votes, the final signature that could still turn to a veto, and he could not decide whether he found it beautiful or infuriating, or whether those were even different reactions. He had wanted to win an argument. Now he understood he was trying to steer something that had a shape before he arrived and would keep its shape after.

April came. In the committee room in the statehouse annex, with badges and folding chairs and a Transportation chair who spoke like she had been born for the role, Parker testified with the exemption in the text and his uncle's route numbers in his notes. The chair called the vote. Three in favor, two against, and his bill moved to the floor calendar, and Parker's hands were shaking so badly he had to press them flat on the table.

"Mr. Chair," said a girl across the room, raising her badge. "Point of information. How many votes will we need up there?"

The chair looked down at her script. "Sixty."

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: The United States baby boom generation was born between 1946 and 1964, and its bulge on the pyramid has now moved into the retirement ages.
story:
Ms. Farah-Ali taped a handout to the whiteboard before the bell had even finished, which Eve took as a threat. The handout showed the population pyramid of the United States, a shape like a wasp that had swallowed a marble, and beneath it the assignment: use the pyramid to predict whether the country will need more schools or more nursing homes, with reasons.

"The bars are ages," said Tayla, leaning over Eve's desk. "Old people on top, babies on the bottom. It's a graph pretending to be a mountain range."

"Then where's the marble?" Eve said. There was a bulge in the middle of the thing, a swelling band of bars that pushed outward around the fifties, sixties, and seventies of age, wider than everything below it. The bars for children were thinner than the bars for their grandparents, which seemed, to Eve, like a mountain range built upside down.

She copied the shape into her notebook anyway, because Ms. Farah-Ali collected notebooks and could sense blank pages the way sharks sense thrashing. After school Eve took the handout to her grandmother's house, where she was expected for dinner and where the assignment was expected to be finished before dessert, house rules being older than she was.

Grandpa was in his recliner watching a documentary about bridges, torpid in the way of a man who had earned it, one slipper on and one slipper mysteriously under the coffee table. Grandmother was in the kitchen being an epicure about a pot of soup, tasting it with a wooden spoon and pronouncing judgment on the salt. Eve spread the pyramid across the kitchen table while the soup muttered.

"That's us," Grandmother said, tapping the bulge with the spoon. "The baby boom. Born 1946 to 1964, all of us, a whole crowd squashed into eighteen years. We've been moving up that chart our whole lives like a pig in a python."

Eve looked at the bulge, which sat in the retirement ages, and looked at her grandmother, who was sixty-eight and ladling soup, and felt something click with an almost audible sensation, as if a lock had been oiled by a spoon. "So the graph already knows you're retired."

"It's known for ages," Grandmother said. "Graphs are patient. It's people who are slow."

Here it is worth admitting what Tayla saw the next morning, because Tayla arrived early to the classroom where Eve sat hunched over her paragraph like a dragon over a small and unimpressive hoard. Tayla read over her shoulder, which was rude, and poked the word "adumbrate" in Eve's draft, which was ruder, because Eve had written that the thin bars at the bottom of the pyramid adumbrated fewer schools, emptying classrooms, and Tayla said, "You can't just put that in to sound smart, that's a war crime."

"It's the right word," Eve said. "The thin bottom shadows what's coming. Fewer kids, so fewer schools. Meanwhile the whole bulge, everyone born 1946 to 1964, has moved into the retirement ages, so nursing homes. More of them. That's my answer. Both are true at once, which Ms. Farah-Ali will probably say is the point."

"Both," Tayla said. "Very diplomatic. Very coward's answer."

"Very correct answer," said Eve, but she frowned at it, because the paragraph bothered her and she could not pin down why. The graph said more nursing homes and fewer schools, but it did not say when, or where, or how a town decides, or what happens to the school when the nursing home wins. The pyramid was honest, but it was honest the way a weather report was honest: it told you the pressure and left you to decide about the umbrella.

Ms. Farah-Ali collected the paragraphs at the end of class and read Eve's with one eyebrow raised, which was her version of applause. "Nursing homes for the boom bulge," she said. "Schools closing at the base. Good. And what can't the pyramid tell you?"

"Whether the people in the bulge want nursing homes," Eve said. "Or whether they'll all move to Florida and ruin your count."

The class laughed, and Ms. Farah-Ali wrote "uncertainty" on the board and underlined it twice, and Eve copied it down next to the wasp-shaped graph, and outside the window somebody's little brother, one thin bar at the bottom of somebody's pyramid, chased a soccer ball across the lot.

That evening Grandmother called to ask whether the soup had helped with the homework. Eve told her she was a bulge, and Grandmother said she had been called worse by better, and asked for her grade.

"Probably an A," Eve said. "But I told them you're going to outlive the graph."

"Of course I am," Grandmother said. "Now write that down."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: An overvote happens when a voter marks more choices than a contest allows, and that vote is not counted for that contest.
story:
The line outside the community hall went twice around the folding tables where the quilters usually met, and Alexia stood in it with her hands in her jacket pockets, watching an old man two places ahead balance his cane on a stack of sample ballots. The hall smelled of floor wax and coffee from the urn the ladies' auxiliary had set up by the door. Maren had texted her three times that morning, all caps, ARE YOU VOTING OR NOT, and Alexia had answered each time with a single word, which was a kind of cowardice she could admit to now, in line, where there was nothing else to do but admit things to herself.

She had turned eighteen exactly six weeks earlier, in September, and had registered the same week at a table outside the library, mostly because Trenton had dared her and partly because her mother had looked at the form and said, in that flat voice she used for anything political, "Your vote doesn't matter, but go ahead." Her mother's stoicism on the subject was total, cultivated over years of disappointment, and Alexia had never been able to tell whether it was wisdom or surrender. Her government teacher, Ms. Toussaint, stood at the opposite pole: she believed in the franchise the way some people believed in weather, as a force you could not argue with, only respond to. Between those two positions Alexia had never quite located herself, and now the line was moving and she still hadn't.

Trenton was already inside when she got through the door. She could see him at the check-in table, arguing cheerfully with a poll worker about whether his signature had changed since he signed the registration card, which it had, because he'd decided in August to write his T's like lightning bolts. He caught sight of her and waved her over with the pen.

"You're late," he said. "I've been a citizen for forty minutes."

"You've been in line for forty minutes." She gave her name to the poll worker, a woman with reading glasses on a beaded chain, and signed her own name, plain, the way she'd signed it since eighth grade, and felt strangely formal doing it.

The booths were cardboard dividers on rented tables, and behind one of them, near the window where the morning light came through in a dusty slant, a girl Alexia didn't know was standing with her pen suspended over the ballot, not moving. Her hand was shaking, just slightly. Alexia slowed down. The girl marked one bubble, then hovered over the bubble next to it, in the same race, and started to fill it in, and Alexia heard herself say, before she'd fully decided to, "Wait."

The girl looked up, startled, pen still touching paper.

"That's the same contest," Alexia said. "You can only pick one there. If you mark two, it's called an overvote, and it doesn't get counted for that contest at all." The words came out steadier than she felt. She had learned it from Ms. Toussaint's class, from a worksheet she'd half done on a Tuesday, and it had seemed like trivia then, something to circle on a quiz, and now it was the most practical thing she knew.

The girl pulled the pen back. "I thought you could rank them," she said. "Like, first choice and second choice."

"Not on this ballot. One race, one bubble." Alexia pointed at the header of the contest, where it said VOTE FOR NOT MORE THAN ONE, which she had read four times herself before understanding that it was addressed to her. "You can get a new ballot if you already messed one up. They have to let you."

The girl exhaled and held up her pen like it was evidence. "I didn't mark it yet. Almost."

"Almost is fine," Alexia said, and the girl laughed, a small wet laugh, and Alexia moved on to her own booth before the moment could get bigger than she could carry.

Alone behind the cardboard, she found that her own hand was not entirely steady either. The ballot was smaller than she had imagined, two sheets, and the races were mostly ones she'd read about in arguments online between people she didn't respect. For the school board there were four candidates and she had liked exactly one of them, a woman who had come to Ms. Toussaint's class in October and answered a hostile question from a disaffected senior without condescension, which had impressed Alexia more than any position paper. For the county commission she had liked none of them, and she sat with her pen down for a long moment, hearing her mother's voice say that not choosing was also a choice, hearing Ms. Toussaint say the opposite, that abstention was how the machine got licensed to ignore you.

What she had figured out, sometime in the last month, mostly on the bus, was that neither of them had the whole answer and that she didn't have to pick a team to have a position. Her mother was right that one vote circumscribes almost nothing; Ms. Toussaint was right that the circumscription was the point, that the lines get drawn by the people who show up. Between those two truths there was room for a person to act anyway, without pretending the act was more or less than it was. She marked the school board race. In the commission race, after another minute, she marked the candidate whose worst position she could at least name, which was a low bar but a real one, and she was honest enough with herself to know that was what it was.

She fed her ballot into the scanner, which swallowed it with a clunk and showed a number ticking upward, and it was that number, 847, that she stood looking at, because it meant there were 846 before her and would be more after, in this one hall, in this one morning, none of them individually decisive, all of them together something.

Outside, Trenton was waiting on the steps with two coffees from the urn, and he handed her one. "So," he said. "Feel different?"

The near-overvote girl was coming down the steps behind them, ballot surrendered, asking a poll worker for a fresh one, and Alexia stepped aside to let her pass.

"No," Alexia said. "I feel exactly the same, except now I've done it."

She held the warm cup against her palm and watched the line still stretching out the door into the parking lot. "Maren's going to be here in twenty minutes. Stay and tell her about the bubbles."

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Stage left and stage right are named from the actor's point of view while facing the audience, so they are the reverse of the audience's left and right.
story:
Lucas had been given the one-act because nobody else wanted it. Ms. Demetriou, who ran the community theatre's young company, had said the word "directing" the way other people said "swimming," as though it were something you could simply fall into, and Lucas had not corrected her. Now he stood in the empty house of the Hartley Street Theatre with a binder of notes he had copied from library books, and on the stage in front of him Declan was going the wrong way for the fourth time.

"Cross left," Lucas called, and Declan crossed right, and Kyler, perched on the edge of the kitchen table that served as the set, laughed in the particular way he had that made you want to excoriate him and also to laugh yourself.

"No, sorry," Lucas said. "House left. My left." Declan walked back, and the moment collapsed again, because Lucas was standing in the audience, facing the stage, and his left was not the stage's left at all. He looked down at his binder. He had written the blocking in the margins the night before, arrows and the letters SL and SR, copied faithfully out of a chapter he had half understood, and now he felt the meaning of those letters rearranging itself in his head like something sedimentary, layer settling against layer, one truth deposited on another.

"Wait," Kyler said. "I read this. Stage left and stage right are from the actor's point of view, facing the audience. So they're the reverse of yours." Declan turned to face the empty seats, raised one hand, and said, "So this is stage right," and it was, and it wasn't the right that Lucas had been shouting for twenty minutes.

"Twenty minutes," Kyler said, not unkindly.

Lucas had imagined directing as a matter of authority. In his imagination he sat in the dark house with a pencil and the actors simply became what he saw, and the pleasure of the fantasy had been, he understood now, mostly the pleasure of not being the one on stage, of being the one who knew. The books had given him a language, but the language was reversed from where he was standing, and he had never noticed because he had never stood anywhere but the audience.

"Let's try it differently," he said. He climbed the steps onto the stage, took Declan's place, and walked the cross himself. "From here, this is stage left." Then he stepped back out into the house and pointed. "From there it's my right, I know, it's backwards, and I should have said so instead of just getting louder." Declan looked at him for a second with an expression Lucas couldn't read, and then nodded once and did the cross cleanly, and Kyler stopped slouching.

They ran the scene until nine. When Ms. Demetriou came through the back door with her coat still on, keys in hand, she watched from the doorway while Declan and Kyler found a rhythm Lucas had not put in the margins, a small pause before Kyler's line that neither of them had planned, and Lucas, standing in the aisle with his binder open, wrote it down.

"Your call," Ms. Demetriou said on her way out. "Keep the pause or cut it?"

Lucas looked at the stage, where the kitchen table sat under the work lights with two coffee cups on it, and at his notebook, where the pause now lived in his handwriting as though it had always been intended. He thought of the night he'd copied the arrows, certain of them, and of how certainty had marched Declan confidently in the wrong direction. He didn't say any of that.

"Keep it," he said. "But I want to see it again from the house before I'm sure."

"Good," she said. "That's the job."

After she left, he locked up, as she'd shown him, the deadbolt first and then the bar across the bottom of the door. Declan and Kyler were already halfway down the block, their voices carrying back to him in pieces, something about auditions in the spring, something about a girl. Lucas stood a moment on the theatre steps with the keys warm in his pocket, thinking that next rehearsal he would stand on the stage when he gave notes, and the one after that in the house, and that he had not yet decided which of those two men he was supposed to be, if he was supposed to be either. The streetlight at the corner buzzed on. He zipped his jacket and went to catch up with them.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: The STAR method answers interview questions about past behavior by describing a Situation, the Task required, the Action you took, and the Result.
story:
Colton had read the phrase three times before he understood it was meant for him: the STAR method answers interview questions about past behavior by describing a Situation, the Task required, the Action you took, and the Result. It sat in the middle of a printout from the library computer, wedged between a paragraph about eye contact and a list of questions employers supposedly loved. He folded it into quarters and put it in his jacket pocket, because the interview was at four, at the Burger Corral on Haldane Road, and it was already twenty past three.

He had wanted the job since March, when he understood what his mother meant by "the margin." The margin was the space between what they had and what the month required, and it kept shrinking. But he had also wanted it for reasons he was less able to say out loud, which was that everyone at school had begun to acquire lives that cost money, and he had begun to feel like a bystander to his own.

Stefan was waiting for him outside the restaurant, leaning on the bike rack with the relaxed authority of someone who had already been employed for five months at the garden centre. "Did you practice?" Stefan asked. "You said you'd practice."

"I read something," Colton said. "In the library. There's a method."

"There's always a method," said Stefan, who believed in methods the way other people believed in weather, which was to say he noticed them but did not think they were about him. Stefan wanted Colton to get this job for his own reasons. He wanted a friend on shift, someone to trade Saturdays with, someone to stand beside during the long empty afternoons when the disaffected customers came through in their slow waves, complaining about pickles. "Tell me the method, then."

Colton unfolded the paper. "The STAR method," he read. "It answers interview questions about past behavior by describing a Situation, the Task required, the Action you took, and the Result." The words came out stiff and rehearsed, like a weather report in a language he was still learning.

Stefan squinted at him. "So like a story with a shape."

Inside, the restaurant smelled of fryer oil and floor cleaner, and the light was the flat white kind that made everything look slightly underwater. A woman at the first register was arguing quietly with a cashier about a missing sauce, and behind her a family of four was negotiating over a menu with the seriousness of a treaty. Colton gave his name to the cashier, who pointed at a booth by the window, and he sat down across from a poster of a milkshake and tried to remember the shape of his own stories.

The manager, Mr. Mokoena, arrived with a clipboard and an unhurried kindness, and he did not sit so much as settle, the way a large animal settles into water. "Colton," he said, checking the page. "Tell me about a time you worked with others toward something difficult."

Colton's mind went entirely blank, then produced, unhelpfully, the image of a documentary he had watched about the ocean floor, the strange communities that lived around thermal vents, an entire biome thriving on nothing but heat and chemistry in the dark. He set the image aside. He thought instead of the group project in tenth grade, the one where Zahra had done most of the research and the other two members had vanished entirely, and where he had received a mark that did not belong to him and had said nothing about it.

"There was a biology project," he began, and then, because the shape was there if he let it be, he followed it. The situation was four students assigned one presentation on river ecosystems. The task was to divide the work and deliver it together. The action, he admitted, was mostly his failure to act: he had not chased the two who disappeared, and he had let Zahra carry the load, though he had at least built the slide deck the night before from her notes. The result was a mark of eighty-one, a grade he had felt sick about for a week, because it debilitated him more than any failure would have, being rewarded for something he had not done.

Mr. Mokoena listened all the way through without writing anything. "Most people tell me the version where they were the hero," he said.

"I could tell you that version," Colton said. "But then I'd have to keep being that person, and I'm not sure I am yet."

Mr. Mokoena almost smiled. "Saturday mornings," he said. "Can you be here at seven?" And he stood, and shook Colton's hand with a dry, careful grip, and went back toward the kitchen, where the fryers hissed like a distant surf.

Outside, the light had gone gold and ordinary. Stefan was still at the bike rack, and Colton told him, and Stefan made a sound of triumph, already planning the Saturdays. Colton felt the weight of the job settle on him, both as money and as something else, a version of himself he would now have to build in public, and he could not yet tell whether the STAR method had helped him or whether he had simply, for once, told the truth in order. He took the folded paper out of his pocket, looked at it, and put it back.

"Seven in the morning," Stefan said. "You're going to hate that."

"I'm going to be there," Colton said, and got on his bike.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The 2026 FIFA World Cup, hosted by Canada, Mexico and the United States, was the first with 48 teams and the first hosted by three countries.
story:
The community field had never held this many people. The rec department had bolted a projector screen to the back of the dugout, and by the second half of the afternoon match the folding chairs had spilled past the foul line, fathers standing along the fence with toddlers on their shoulders. Ryder sat on the grass between his father and Kathryn, a paper plate of samosas balanced on his knee, watching the broadcast flicker whenever someone walked in front of the lens.

Susan arrived late, jacket half on, and dropped down beside Kathryn with the confidence of someone who had opinions ready. "They shouldn't even be playing this many teams," she said, nodding at the screen. "Forty-eight. It's a mistake. More matches, more nonsense, worse football."

"It's not a mistake, it's the format," Kathryn said. "This one's different. Forty-eight teams for the first time."

"First time ever?"

"First time in the World Cup, obviously," Kathryn said, and stole a samosa.

Susan looked past her to Ryder, because Ryder was the one who actually kept these things straight, the one who could recite squads like scripture. "Tell her it dilutes it," Susan said. "Tell her a tournament that big isn't special anymore."

Ryder took a moment, because the honest answer was not the one either of them wanted. "It's the first with forty-eight," he said. "But it's also the first with three hosts. Canada, Mexico, the United States. All three together. So it's not just a bigger tournament, it's a wider one." He shrugged. "I used to think those were the same argument. They're not."

Susan rolled her eyes at the fence. Mr. Siddiqui, who coached the under-tens and had set up the screen himself, laughed from his lawn chair without turning around. "He does this," he said. "Sits on the fence until the fence is comfortable."

The match resumed, and the argument dissolved the way theirs always did, into shouting at a linesman. Ryder watched a midfielder receive the ball with her back to goal, shield it, turn, and lose it, and win it back again before anyone could punish her, and he thought about what his father kept saying on the drive over, that the game was their patrimony, something handed down, and how his father meant a specific version of it: the old formats, the old scarcity, the tournament you waited four years for because missing it would inure you to nothing but disappointment. His father had grown up with one host country at a time and treated the change like a debt against the sport itself. Ryder half believed him. He also remembered the qualification highlights from June, small nations arriving at tournaments they had never reached, and how that had felt like the opposite of dilution, though he couldn't prove it, and knew Susan would say it was sentiment dressed up as analysis.

The truth, as far as he could hold it, was that both things were real. The tournament was bigger and messier and some group-stage games would be forgettable, and also more of the world was inside it now, and the two facts had to be carried together, like two full cups walked across a crowded field. He hadn't worked out the arithmetic of which mattered more. He suspected there was no arithmetic, only taste, and he hated settling for that.

At the break, his father came back from the concession table with two lemonades and handed one down to him. "Susan says you told her the new format is fine."

"I didn't say fine. I said it's the first one with three hosts, and forty-eight teams, and I don't know yet if that's worse."

His father looked at him for a long second, the way he looked at a defensive line before a free kick. "Huh," he said, and sat down, and after a while, without conceding anything, he said, "That Canadian keeper is something, though. Watch her positioning."

Susan leaned over Kathryn's shoulder toward Ryder. "So if it's three countries, who gets the final?"

Ryder shook his head. "Don't know that one."

"Ascetic about your facts, then," Kathryn said, grinning. "Only believing what you can prove."

"Someone has to be," Ryder said, and pointed at the screen as the players walked back out, because the second half was starting and the keeper was already crouched low on her line, tapping each post twice, the crowd rising behind her all the way down the fence and out past the foul line into the grass.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: In a fixed-payment loan, each payment's interest is charged on the remaining balance, so early payments go more toward interest and later payments more toward principal.
story:
The loan statement came in a plain envelope, and Elliot's mother set it on the kitchen table between the salt shaker and a bowl of peaches, the way she set down things she didn't want to talk about yet. Elliot could see the numbers through the thin paper when the lamp hit it. He was eighteen in six days, and he had been the one who told her the car was a good idea, so he made himself pick it up.

"Fourteen payments made," he read aloud. "Balance of..." He stopped, subtracted, and subtracted again as if arithmetic were the problem. "Mom. We've paid over four thousand dollars and the balance only went down by about nine hundred."

She dried her hands on a dish towel and sat down across from him. "That's what the man at the dealership kept saying. Fixed payments. Same amount every month, easy to budget."

Something was wrong with that, and Elliot could feel the wrongness without being able to name it, like hearing a piano key that had gone flat. He got his notebook, the one he'd been using to parametrize his summer budget, each expense a variable he could turn up or down. He'd assumed the loan was one variable too, a fixed thing. "If we paid four thousand and only nine hundred stuck," he said slowly, "then three thousand went somewhere else."

Nova arrived at the back door without knocking, the way she always did when her own house got too quiet, and slid into the third chair. "What are we doing?"

"Solving a crime," Elliot said. "The money keeps disappearing."

She pulled the statement toward her and ran her finger down the columns. "Okay, look. Interest. Every month there's an interest charge, and it's big at the top and it gets smaller as you go down. And the principal part, the part that actually reduces the balance, starts small and grows." She tapped the last row. "It's not that they're stealing. Each payment's interest is charged on the remaining balance, so the early payments go more toward interest and the later ones more toward principal."

"So we're paying mostly interest right now," Elliot said.

"For the beginning of the loan, yeah. The end of the loan is where you finally get ahead."

His mother looked out the window at the car, a gray hatchback she drove to the early shift at the hospital, and Elliot understood that what he was feeling was not math. It was that he had sold her something. He had done the grandiose version of the math, the one where the car meant she'd stop taking the bus at 4:40 in the morning, and he had never once asked what the borrowing itself would cost. He'd thought interest was a fee, a flat toll, when actually it was alive, feeding on whatever was left.

"I did the savings thing wrong too, didn't I," he said. He got his phone and opened the account where he'd put his graduation money, two hundred dollars a month from the garden center job, meant for the deposit on an apartment near campus. The interest line was small and embarrassing. But it was on the right side of the ledger. Every month the bank charged the balance a little and added it to the balance, so the same deposit meant more over time, not less. He'd been treating the two accounts like they were unrelated. "It's the same force," he said. "Both directions."

"What's the same force?" Zane stood in the doorway, holding a bike helmet and a bag of chips he'd clearly brought for himself.

"Interest," Nova said. "It's why my mom's car took forever to pay off, and it's why my grandma keeps saying time in the market matters. It pushes both ways."

Zane dropped into the chair and stole a peach. "Cool. Can we eat?"

Elliot ignored him. He spread the notebook flat and drew two arrows, one labeled loan and one labeled savings, both bending away from zero in opposite directions. Then he crossed out the savings arrow, thought about it, and drew it back in, longer. "Here's what I keep not knowing," he said. "If I put extra toward the loan, the balance drops, and then next month's interest is smaller because there's less balance to charge. But if I put that same money in savings, the interest compounds for four years while I'm at school. I can't do both. I don't know which wins."

Ms. Marino, who had come over to return a casserole dish and had been standing quietly by the counter for most of it, set the dish in the sink. "When I was your age I got that wrong twice," she said. "Once in each direction."

"So there's no rule?"

"There's arithmetic. Whether it comforts you is a separate question." She took a peach for herself. "If you ever want to run the numbers, my kitchen table is free."

After she left, and after Zane had eaten his way through the chips and gone home, Elliot's mother stayed at the table with him. He showed her the two arrows. He said he could take his next two paychecks and put them on the loan, and after that the interest would be smaller every month, and if she matched him even a little, it would move faster still. He said he wasn't sure it beat the savings account, and he said that honestly, and she didn't seem to mind the uncertainty, or maybe she was just tired.

"Eighteen on Saturday," she said. "What do you want?"

"To pay it down with you. Starting this week." He closed the notebook and slid it across the table to her, the two arrows still showing, and she put her hand flat on the cover like she was keeping the pages from blowing away.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Sorting a list takes more work than one linear search, so sorting just to run binary search pays off only when the same data will be searched many times.
story:
Logan had forty minutes before the coding club deadline, and his screen was showing him a list of two thousand book titles, unsorted, mocking him in alphabetical chaos. The regional competition wanted their program to look up whether a requested title was in stock, fast, and Logan had spent the whole week falling in love with binary search. You cut the list in half, then in half again, and again, until the answer appeared in a handful of steps instead of two thousand slow peeks. He understood the appeal the way he understood chess: elegance born of order.

"Sorted yet?" Loic dropped into the chair beside him, unwrapping a granola bar that smelled faintly of fake strawberries. Behind them, Ammar was arguing with the vending machine, which had eaten his dollar and given him nothing but a ominous mechanical pause.

"Almost," Logan lied. "The sort is the boring part. The search is the beautiful part. Ten steps, maybe twelve, instead of reading every single entry like a sad librarian."

"So sort it and go beautiful," Loic said, crumbs landing on Logan's keyboard like tiny punishments.

Here was the snag, and Logan had only begun to feel it, an inchoate suspicion that had not yet found words. He sat back. "How many times does the demo actually search?"

"Once, I think. It asks for one book, prints found or not found, done."

The suspicion crystallized into something with teeth. Sorting was itself a kind of labor, a long process of comparisons and swaps, and doing all that work to run a single search was like renovating an entire house because you needed to open one door. The linear search, plodding and unglamorous, would just walk up to that one door directly. Logan stared at his sort function, which he had named `glorious_sort` an hour earlier, and felt the glory draining out of it. He could admit the mathematics had seduced him. Sorting a list takes more work than one linear search, he realized, so sorting just to run a binary search only pays off when the same data gets searched many times. One search meant the ugly method won.

"I've been worshipping the wrong god," he announced.

Loic looked up. "Which god?"
