"Elegance. For one lookup, the dumb slow scan is actually faster overall. My sort costs more than it saves."

Ammar arrived, defeated, dollar-less, and overheard enough to frown. "That can't be right. Binary search is the good one. Mr. Karimi said so."

"Mr. Karimi said it's the good one on sorted data," Logan said, and enjoyed saying it, because for once he had the teacher's exact phrasing in his pocket. "It's not the sorting's bodyguard. It doesn't defend the sort's honor."

From the doorway, Mr. Karimi coughed in a way that suggested he had heard his own name used as currency. He did not explain anything, which was his way. He only set a printed page on the table, folded once, and pointed at a line near the bottom, then wandered off toward the coffee machine as though the whole thing bored him profoundly.

The page was the final judging rubric, which none of them had read past the first section because the first section had mentioned pizza coupons. Near the bottom, in merciless twelve-point font, was the test protocol: the program would be run against a stream of a hundred queries against the same catalog, scored on total time.

From there it was Loic who watched things happen, because Logan's face was doing something remarkable. Loic had seen Logan smug, Logan defeated, Logan deeply asleep in physics, but never Logan caught between two truths, delighted and betrayed at once. His inchoate theology had collapsed into a genuinely funny position: the sort he had almost deleted was now essential, and the dumb linear scan he had just defended with real passion was suddenly the wrong answer.

"So," Loic said slowly, savoring it, "five minutes ago the sort was a waste. Now it's the hero. What do you actually believe, Logan? You can't absolve the sort just because the rubric changed its mind."

Logan laughed, a startled bark that made Ammar jump. "That's the thing. I believe both. One search, linear wins. A hundred searches, sort first. It's like utilitarianism, sort of, except the happiness is speed and you have to know how many people are coming to dinner before you know whether to cook."

"That's a terrible analogy," Ammar said.

"It's an inchoate analogy. Give it time."

They rebuilt the program in half an hour, Logan typing, Ammar calling out typos, Loic eating a second granola bar over everyone's objections. `glorious_sort` stayed, restored to favor, though Logan renamed it `necessary_sort` with visible reluctance. The binary search itself was eight lines, so clean it almost glittered, and when it found its first test title in nine steps, Ammar applauded with two mechanical pencil halves.

Mr. Karimi drifted back with his coffee and stood behind them, reading the screen over Logan's shoulder. Logan tensed, waiting for a verdict, a lesson, something quotable.

Mr. Karimi took a sip. "You argue with your code out loud, Mr. Logan. The whole floor heard you absolve a sorting algorithm."

"It deserved it," Logan said. "Then it deserved the opposite."

"Then run it," said Mr. Karimi, and tapped the edge of the screen, where the cursor blinked, waiting on a hundred queries and a clock.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Artists commonly keep two versions of their statement: a short one of about 50 to 100 words and a longer one of about 500 to 1,000 words.
story:
The grass was still wet when Ava carried the ninth painting out to the picnic table, propping it against the fence beside the others. From the kitchen window her mother had asked, twice, why she couldn't do this inside, and twice Ava had said the light was better, which was true, though not the whole reason. Indoors the paintings argued with the wallpaper and the grocery list on the fridge. Out here, arranged in a crooked row between the tomato stakes and Diego's old basketball hoop, they looked almost like something.

The theme was doors. She had decided that in September, back when it had seemed like a clever constraint rather than a cage, and since then she had painted a screen door bitten by hail, the gap under her grandmother's hospital room, a bus door closing on a stranger's sleeve. Nine down. One to go, and then the statement, which Mr. Flores had mentioned only in passing, the way he mentioned most things, as though the real work should already be obvious.

Diego came through the side gate carrying two bottles of orange soda, because he believed every serious occasion required refreshment. He walked the row slowly, hands in his pockets, and stopped at the hail painting. "That one's the best one. It looks like the door got old overnight."

"Everything got old overnight." Ava took a soda anyway. The last three weeks of the semester had settled over her like weather, a low gray ennui she couldn't point to any single cause for. Even the word felt borrowed until she was standing in front of her own paintings and could not remember which of them she had liked.

"Still need one more?"

"And the statement." She said it flatly, testing how bad it sounded out loud. "For the portfolio. Ten pieces, one theme, plus an artist's statement explaining the whole thing."

Diego twisted his cap off with his shirt hem, which was disgusting, and drank. "So write it. You're loquacious enough. You wrote a page on why the vending machine needed better snacks."

"That's the problem. I don't know how long it's supposed to be. Mr. Flores said the gallery in November wants a statement for the wall cards, but the art school application wants one too, and I keep imagining a gallery visitor standing there for forty minutes reading my entire life story taped next to a painting of a screen door."

Diego considered this with the gravity he usually reserved for penalty calls. "You could ask Carlos. His sister applied to art school last year. She got in."

Carlos was reachable in the way only Carlos was, which was instantly, as though he had been sitting by his phone waiting for a question about artist statements. His voice came through the speaker propped against the ketchup bottle. "Oh yeah, that's a whole thing. She kept two versions. A short one for the wall card, like fifty to a hundred words, and a long one for the application, around five hundred to a thousand words. Artists do that all the time."

"Two versions of the same statement?"

"Same statement, different lengths. Nobody reads a wall card that's a thousand words long. But the application people want to know you can think in full."

Ava sat down on the picnic table bench, the wet of it soaking through her shorts, and looked at her doors again. Something in the row rearranged itself in her head, the way a sentence does when you finally hear its rhythm. The short version wasn't a summary of the long version. It was a different kind of thinking, the way a sketch wasn't a smaller painting. Fifty to a hundred words was a doorway you walked through in a second. Five hundred to a thousand was a room you could actually stand in. And maybe that was the whole theme, she thought, and then made herself stop thinking it, because a thought like that could ferment into something either very good or very convenient, and she couldn't yet tell which.

"Did she hate writing them?" Ava asked.

"She said the short one was harder. You have to know what you actually believe."

That night, after Diego left and the paintings were stacked in the garage against the coming dew, Ava sat cross-legged on the picnic table with a notebook and wrote the long one first, because it was the cowardly order. She wrote about doors as thresholds, about the moment before entering, about her grandmother's hospital door and the sleeve caught in the bus, about how a door is the only object that is both wall and invitation depending on the second. Nine hundred words, which she counted, and which surprised her, because she had assumed she had less to say than that.

Then she tried the short one and crossed out six beginnings. The long statement had let her circle; the short one demanded she land somewhere. She wrote "I paint doors because we never get to see both sides at once," looked at it, and could not decide if it was true or merely tidy. She underlined it twice, which was her system for words she did not trust yet, and went inside.

In the morning the grass was wet again, and Mr. Flores was at the fence, dropping off a crate of peppers his brother had grown too many of. He looked over the fence at the garage, where the ninth painting leaned visible in the open door. "Nine?"

"Nine and a half. I'm repainting the bus one. The sleeve was wrong."

He nodded slowly, the way he did when a student had skipped past the easy answer, and handed her a pepper through the fence slats. "Bring the half one on Monday anyway. Sometimes the wrong sleeve is the right one."

She stood holding the pepper, looking down the row of the garage at all her doors, and said, "Do you think a theme has to mean one thing?"

He was already walking back toward his house, but he turned, and considered, and put his hands in his pockets. "Ask me again when there's ten."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: The Situation-Behavior-Impact model, from the Center for Creative Leadership, frames feedback by naming when it happened, what the person did, and what effect it had.
story:
Isaac had said the word to Tomas's face, "lazy," and it had landed like a dropped oar.

The canoes were already loaded on the trailer by the time the waterfront director pulled him aside. Cabin seven was Isaac's to lead that week, and Tomas was in it, and for three days Tomas had been the last to the dock every morning, dragging his paddle, complaining about the cold. On Thursday, when Tomas was late again and the others had to wait, Isaac had turned around on the wet planks and said it. Lazy. Nobody begged him to take it back. Rania, who had co-led the cabin with him all summer, only looked at the water, and Tomas didn't speak for the rest of the afternoon.

That night, in the empty staff room above the boathouse, Rania sat across from him with a mug of tea going cold between her hands. "I want to run the overnight with a cabin that isn't falling apart," she said. "That's all I want right now. So fix it, or I'll do it badly, and then nobody's happy." She wasn't angry. That was somehow worse. "You told him what he is. That's not a thing you know."

Isaac turned his phone over on the table. Earlier, trying to find the words to apologize, he had searched something like "how to give feedback" and fallen into a turgid article about management theory, pages of it, thick with jargon that seemed designed to confuse. But near the end there had been one small usable thing, a model from the Center for Creative Leadership. He showed Rania the screen. "It's called Situation-Behavior-Impact," he said. "You name when it happened, what the person did, and what effect it had. That's the whole thing."

"So instead of lazy," Rania said, slowly, the way she worked through a hard passage of music, "it would be, yesterday morning, you came to the dock ten minutes late, and the rest of us waited and we lost the calm water."

"Something like that." He looked at the sentence she had just said, testing its syntax in his mouth, the pieces in their order, situation and behavior and impact, each one doing its job. It seemed almost too simple. And yet it changed what the sentence was. It was no longer a verdict on Tomas's soul, which Isaac had no right to deliver, only a report of one morning, which he had watched with his own eyes.

He found Tomas the next morning at breakfast, sitting at the end of the bench with his tray. The lake outside the window was flat and bright, and somewhere down the hill the kitchen radio was playing something soft. Isaac sat down without asking, which was itself a kind of statement.

"Yesterday was unfair," Isaac said. "What I said. I don't get to decide what you are." Tomas kept cutting his pancake into smaller and smaller pieces. Isaac went on, feeling for each word like a handrail in the dark. "Wednesday morning, everyone else was on the dock at eight, and you came at ten past, and we missed the still water on the east shore. When you're late, the whole cabin pays for it. That's what I should have said."

Tomas was quiet long enough that Isaac began composing his retreat. Then Tomas said, "I'm not late because I don't care. I can't sleep in the bunk room. Ariella's fan clicks." He said it in a low voice, and Isaac realized with a small shame that he had never once asked. "I was lying awake until two and then I'd oversleep and then I'd come down already knowing everyone was angry at me."

There was the thing Isaac hadn't seen. The model gave him the form of an honest sentence, but the sentence was only half of it; the other half was listening long enough to have something true to put inside. "We can move your bunk," Isaac said. "And I'll tell the group the lateness is being handled, not that it's who you are."

At the overnight two nights later, they paddled out in the last light, Tomas in the bow of Isaac's canoe, on time, half asleep but there. Rania, in the next boat, called across the water that the sunset was beguiling them all into staying out too long, and they laughed, and turned back while the east was still pale. Tomas's paddle dipped and rose without complaint, catching the light, and the shore came slowly toward them through the dark water.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: A security deposit is held to cover unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear, so in many jurisdictions a landlord cannot deduct for ordinary aging like small nail holes.
story:
The apartment smelled like cardboard and old coffee, and Alyssa stood in the middle of it with her phone raised, photographing the wall beside the window for the third time. Zackary's whole life was in boxes by the door, and the walls he was leaving behind were pocked with small nail holes where his posters had hung for two years.

"He says he's keeping part of the deposit," Zackary said, waving a printed email. "Four hundred dollars for repainting. For nail holes, Alyssa. Nail holes."

Zachary, the roommate, sat on the counter eating cereal out of the box. "My dad says that's what deposits are for. They just take it."

Alyssa lowered the phone. "That's not what it's for. My aunt lost a whole deposit when I was twelve and she talked about it for like a year. A security deposit is held to cover unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear. Nail holes are just the wall aging. It's ordinary." She said it with more certainty than she felt, because she had read it at two in the morning on a tenants' rights site, and reading a thing at two in the morning was not the same as knowing it.

She went to the window and kept shooting anyway, every scuff and every hole, because if the landlord disputed her reading of the rules she wanted a record. The kitchen tap dripped while she worked, a small tin sound, and through the open window someone was frying onions four floors down.

Zackary read the email aloud while she photographed. The landlord, a Ms. Sutherland who owned the building outright and had paid off the mortgage decades ago, claimed the walls required "professional restoration." Alyssa had learned that word two weeks ago, when Zackary explained why his rent went up every year while Ms. Sutherland's costs did not. She owns it, he had said. The bank got its money back years ago and now she just collects. Alyssa had thought about her own parents, still sending checks to a lender in another state, thirty years into a down payment that had been scraped together from two jobs and a loan from an uncle. Renting had seemed like throwing money away until she understood that her parents had paid twice the price of the house for the privilege of paying slowly. She had not resolved which was worse. She suspected it depended on money you had.

"Write back," she said. "Tell her you have photographs from move-in and move-out, and that small nail holes are normal wear, and you expect the full deposit back."

"I don't want to burn a bridge," Zackary said. "I need her as a reference."

"So don't burn it. Be polite. Being polite and being a doormat aren't the same thing."

That night, sitting on the floor of her own room with the radiator ticking beside her, Alyssa drafted the message on Zackary's behalf and texted it to him, then sat with her chin on her knees while the radiator ticked and the smell of dust rose warm off the metal fins. "Dear Ms. Sutherland," she had written, "thank you for two years at the property. I've attached photographs documenting the walls at move-in and now, at move-out. As I understand it, a deposit covers unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear, and small nail holes are ordinary aging rather than damage. I'd appreciate the return of the full deposit, and I'm glad to walk the apartment with you before I return the keys." She read it four times. It sounded firm and it sounded courteous and she could not tell whether it sounded like an eighteen-year-old who had read a website once, or like someone with a lawyer.

Ms. Sutherland replied the next morning: a single line, brisk and unbothered, saying she would meet them at four and bring the checkbook.

They stood in the empty apartment together, the late sun laying a long orange stripe across the floorboards where the couch used to be. Ms. Sutherland moved along the walls in her good coat, and Alyssa held up her phone at each hole, preempting the objection before it could form, showing the move-in photo and the move-out photo side by side. Small holes then, small holes now, a few more of them.

"You've done this before," Ms. Sutherland said.

"No," Alyssa said. "I read."

Ms. Sutherland looked at the wall for a long moment, then at the checkbook in her hand, and Zachary, still crunchy with cereal dust on his sleeves, held the door open with his foot.

"Full deposit," Ms. Sutherland said, writing. "The place was cheap because of the walk-up, not because of the walls."

Zackary took the check with both hands, like something breakable, and Alyssa pocketed her phone, the photographs still on the screen, the radiator already cold.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Socialist politician Jean Jaurès wrote a socialist history of the French Revolution in the early 1900s that shaped the class-conflict interpretation dominant for much of the twentieth century.
story:
Grayson sat at the kitchen table with three books fanned open in front of him and a blank document glowing on the laptop screen, cursor pulsing in the top corner of an empty page. The assignment was due Thursday: an essay on how interpretations of the French Revolution had changed since 1800. He understood, in a vague and annoying way, that people had argued about the Revolution for two centuries, but every time he tried to write the first sentence, it extruded itself into something pompous, like "Throughout history, historians have debated history," which he deleted after reading it twice and feeling embarrassed both times.

His mother set a plate of sliced apple and cheese beside the keyboard without asking whether he wanted it, because she knew he would not notice hunger until ten at night. "You've been staring at that screen since four," she said. "Blink once in a while."

"I'm blinking," he said. "I'm blinking a lot. It's just not helping."

The problem, as far as he could tell, was that the books didn't disagree about facts. They disagreed about what the facts were for. One author treated the Revolution as a catastrophe, the work of ideologues who drowned France in blood for abstractions. Another treated it as the necessary, if messy, birth of modern democracy. A third, a thick French book the library had produced from the basement, kept returning to grain prices and bread riots and the word "bourgeois" as though it explained everything. Grayson couldn't tell whether the third author was more scientific or just more committed.

The doorbell rang at seven and Ariel came in carrying her own essay materials, which consisted of one notebook and a confidence Grayson envied. Domenico followed, holding his phone out like a lantern. "Okay, you have to see this," Domenico said. "My grandpa's town. We walked past it on the way to the bakery, and I took a picture because the name looked like ours." He dropped into the chair across from Grayson and slid the phone over. It showed a weathered stone memorial, a column of carved names, and near the bottom a plaque with a single line beneath one of them.

"Who is he?" Grayson asked.

"No idea. Some guy from the town. Grandpa said he was a politician who got assassinated in 1914, right before the war. That's all he knew."

Grayson read the name twice. Jean Jaurès. He typed it into the laptop, half expecting a minor local figure, a mayor or a deputy. The results filled the screen, and he sat back. "He's not just a politician," he said slowly. "He wrote a whole history of the Revolution. A socialist history. In the early 1900s."

"A socialist wrote a history?" Ariel leaned over his shoulder, and her hair fell against his arm, and he was careful not to move. "How do you write a history that's socialist?"

"Same way you write one that's royalist, I guess." Grayson scrolled. The book was called something like A Socialist History of the French Revolution, and it had run to multiple volumes, decades of work. Jaurès had been a socialist politician, a real one, elected, arguing in parliament, and he had also been a historian, and the two things had gone into the same book. "Listen to this," Grayson said. "People say his interpretation, the class-conflict one, dominated for most of the twentieth century. Like, this is the lens everybody looked through." He turned in his chair. "My third book. The bourgeois book. That's where it comes from."

"Wait." Ariel pulled her notebook toward her. "So the guy on Domenico's memorial is the reason your book sounds like that?"

"That's what it's saying." Grayson read further, but carefully, the way Mr. Moretti had told them to read secondary sources, asking who was writing and when and what they wanted. He did not want to get it wrong in an essay. He tried drafting a sentence: the class-conflict interpretation, shaped by Jaurès, remained dominant for much of the twentieth century. He looked at it. It was accurate and it was flat. He deleted "remained" and tried "became," then put "remained" back.

"So what's your essay about now?" Domenico asked, retrieving his phone and looking at the plaque again with new interest, as if the stone itself had rearranged itself into something more important.

"I don't know yet. That's the honest answer." Grayson pulled the keyboard closer. "I thought I had to pick a side, like the Revolution was good or bad, and I kept stalling because I don't think I can pick. But maybe the essay isn't about picking. Maybe it's about why each generation sees what it needs to see. The conservatives after 1800 wanted order, so they saw chaos. The republicans wanted citizenship, so they saw rights. Jaurès wanted justice for workers, so he saw class conflict, and everyone after him looked through his window for decades." He stopped, hearing himself, worried it sounded effusive, too much like a speech. He muted it on the page: fewer adjectives, more dates, a concession sentence admitting that where the interpretations overlapped, the Revolution had still actually happened, people had still actually died, whatever lens you held up.

His mother came through with laundry balanced on her hip and paused long enough to read the opening paragraph over his shoulder. "That's better than the blinking," she said, and kept walking. Ariel slid the apple plate toward herself and Domenico without comment, dividing it, and Grayson kept typing. He did not know yet what his final position would be, only that it would have to carry the uncertainty with it, honestly, in plain sentences. At the bottom of the document he typed a note to himself: ask Mr. Moretti whether honesty about not knowing counts as a thesis.

Around nine, Ariel closed her notebook and said she had to be home. Domenico stood, then stopped, pointing at the screen. "Put the memorial in."

"What?"

"Describe the plaque. Start there." He pulled on his jacket. "It's a real thing. Everything else is just books."

Grayson looked at the empty top of the page, then at the photo Domenico had texted him, the stone column and the small plaque and the name carved under the year 1914. He began to type: In a small town in France, on a war memorial, there is the name of Jean Jaurès.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: MLA style cites sources in the text with the author's name and page number in parentheses, and lists the full sources at the end under the heading 'Works Cited'.
story:
John's grandfather's kitchen smelled of scorched coffee and newsprint, and the table under the window was the only surface in the house wide enough for a laptop, a library book, and a plate of toast without anything falling off. He had been exiled here for the weekend because his mother had decided his room needed painting, and because his history paper was due Monday, and because his grandfather had a printer that still worked despite being older than John.

The paper was supposed to argue something, which was the first problem. In Ms. Robinson's English class he had learned that a paper made a claim and defended it, and that when you borrowed an idea you put the author's name and page number in parentheses right there in your sentence, like a receipt. Then he had switched into the history class at midterm, and the teacher kept returning his drafts with one word circled in red at the bottom: bibliography. John had written "Works Cited." He had written it three times now. Each time it came back, and each time he felt the strange injustice of being marked wrong for something that had been right one hallway over.

He typed a sentence about Marcus Aurelius, deleted it, and typed it again. The library book beside his elbow was a biography of the emperor, its spine cracked at the chapters on the wars, and John had chosen stoicism as his topic partly because it interested him and mostly because there was exactly one book about it in the house. His grandfather, who had so far contributed only coffee refills, drifted past the table and stopped.

"Stoicism," his grandfather said, reading over John's shoulder. "I wrote a paper on that once."

"Everybody wrote a paper on that once," John said, and his grandfather laughed and went back to the stove without absolving him of anything, which was fair, since John hadn't finished a paragraph yet.

He texted Adrienne, who was in the same history class and had somehow already absorbed its rules. "what does he want instead of works cited," he typed. She answered fast, between what he assumed were her own toast and her own despair. "bibliography. it's a history class. mine still says works cited too btw, i just found out." Then a second message: "for english mla still does author name and page number in parentheses, the full sources go at the end under Works Cited." John read it twice. So the two classes wanted the same honesty arranged differently, one teacher collecting receipts inline, the other wanting the ledger at the back, and he had been arguing with a heading as if it were a principle.

He was halfway through retitling the page when his grandfather came back and set down a shoebox. "You said everybody wrote one," he said. "Here's mine." Inside, soft with age, was a paper typed on actual onionskin, the pages full of small numbers riding above the line, and at the bottom of each page the numbered notes themselves, citations in a style John had never seen, formal and antiquated, everything a scholar owed tucked away at the foot of the text like a confession. His grandfather had been in college before MLA was even the air everyone breathed in English departments. John hadn't known his grandfather had been in college at all.

"Can I read it?" John said.

"It's not good," his grandfather said. "It argues that Marcus Aurelius was a hypocrite because he wrote about accepting fate while fighting a war to keep his throne. My professor said it was too clever by half." He said this with obvious pride, and John, skimming the last page, found the argument sharper than that, more honest, the kind that admits at the end what it cannot prove. There was a paragraph about uncertainty, about whether a man could believe in stoicism and still have it both ways, and the old paper declined to resolve it. John felt the odd vertigo of discovering that his grandfather had once been sixteen and sweating over a due date, and had arrived at a question rather than an answer, and had apparently considered that fine.

He pulled his laptop closer and typed the sentence again, this time keeping it. The paper would argue that Marcus Aurelius's journals showed a real philosophy under real political pressure, and it would concede, in the last paragraph, that no footnote could settle whether the emperor meant any of it. He moved his inline citations into the shape the history class wanted, or near enough, and changed the heading to Bibliography, and under the heading he listed the biography and, after a pause, his grandfather's onionskin pages, cited as best he could invent, because they belonged at the back of the paper even if no style manual on earth had a rule for them.

"What did you decide?" his grandfather asked, collecting the coffee cup.

"About Marcus?" John saved the file. "That he meant it. Mostly. I put the mostly in the last paragraph."

"Too clever by half," his grandfather said, but he was smiling at the shoebox, and he slid it across the table, closer to John's elbow, next to the printer that still worked.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Compound or coating chocolate, which replaces some or all cocoa butter with other fats, sets without tempering but does not have the same snap.
story:
Mathis had the thermometer in one hand and his phone in the other, propped against the sugar canister, a video paused at the part where the chef said the words "seed crystals" as though everyone at home already knew what they meant. On the counter sat two pounds of dark chocolate, chopped into uneven pieces, and a stainless steel bowl over a pan of barely simmering water. He was doing this because his mother had said, back in March, that if he wanted a job at the pâtisserie on Rue Sainte-Anne he would have to show them something, and because he had decided, quietly, that the something would be a bar of chocolate so glossy it looked like lacquer.

The first attempt had bloomed. He had melted everything, poured it into the mold, waited, and pulled out a bar that was dull as chalk and bent like an eraser when he tried to snap it. He had eaten the evidence standing at the sink, which felt like a small defeat he could at least taste.

Now he was trying again, and Harmony was there, sitting on the counter with her sneakers knocking against the cabinet, because she had wandered over after her shift and refused to leave. "You're stirring it a lot," she observed.

"That's the point. You melt it to forty-five, cool it to twenty-seven while stirring, bring it back up to thirty-one. If you hold it there, it sets shiny and it snaps." He said the numbers like a catechism, though he could not have said why those temperatures and not others. That bothered him more than he admitted. The video gave procedure; the reasoning underneath, the actual physics, he only half followed.

"Sounds like a religion," Harmony said.

"Sounds like a chemistry grade I didn't get."

The chocolate reached forty-five degrees and he pulled the bowl off the heat, added a fistful of unmelted chunks, and began the slow work of cooling it down, stirring in small circles, scraping the sides. The kitchen smelled like something between a bakery and a forest floor, dense and faintly bitter. From the window over the sink they could see the montane ridge behind town, still holding snow in the shaded gullies even this late in the season, and Harmony kept glancing at it as though it owed her money.

"My cousin did this at the campsite last summer," she said. "She had those candy melts, the little buttons, and she just melted them in a bag in hot water and dipped everything. Pretzels, strawberries. They set up hard on the picnic table in like ten minutes. No thermometer, none of this." She waved at the thermometer, the bowls, the whole liturgy of it.

Mathis kept stirring, but slower. "Those aren't really chocolate," he said. "Not the way this is. Compound or coating chocolate replaces some or all of the cocoa butter with other fats. That's why she didn't need to temper it. It sets on its own." He had read that somewhere three days ago, at two in the morning, and it had struck him as both obvious and slightly fraudulent. "But it doesn't have the same snap. You bite it and it kind of waxes."

"So my cousin's pretzels were fake."

"They were easy." He tested the chocolate against his lower lip, which the video said was a better instrument than the wrist. Barely warm. Twenty-seven, or close. He put the bowl back over the water for ten seconds, fifteen, watching the thermometer climb toward thirty-one the way the ridge climbed toward the snowline.

He poured. The mold was a cheap silicone thing he had ordered online, and the chocolate ran into the rectangles in thick ribbons, and he tapped the mold on the counter to knock the air bubbles out, tap after tap, until his palm stung. Harmony slid off the counter to hold it steady.

While it set, they sat on the floor with their backs against the cabinets and split one of the failed bars from attempt one, the bloomed one, which still tasted like chocolate even though it looked like a mistake. "Here's what I can't decide," Mathis said. "The candy melts are honest, in a way. They do what they say. Melt, dip, done. No ritual. And this," he gestured at the mold on the counter, at the thermometer drying on the rack, "this is me trusting a procedure I don't fully understand because people who do understand it vouch for it. My epistemology here is basically the comments section under that video."

"You watched the whole thing, though."

"Twice." He chewed. "But that's the thing. The recipe works even if I can't derive it. And my cousin's way works too, for what it is. Maybe you pick your difficulty on purpose. Maybe wanting the snap is the whole point, and the snap costs this." He wasn't sure the position held together, and he said so, and Harmony said that was fair, and they left it there, unfinished, like most of the good arguments they had.

After twenty minutes in the cool of the pantry, he turned the mold over and pressed the bottom with his thumbs. The bars dropped out one by one, and each one caught the overhead light and threw it back.

Harmony took one, held it to her ear, and snapped it in half. The break was clean and loud, like a small branch.

"Okay," she said, and reached for another.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: The STAR method structures an interview answer as Situation, Task, Action and Result, so a story about past experience ends with what actually happened.
story:
Michael had always considered himself excellent under pressure, which was one of the many things about Michael that nobody else had ever considered. So when the grocery store on Halsted posted a HELP WANTED sign in green marker, he told Tanner he would have the job by Friday, and Tanner, who had heard predictions like this before, said only, "Sure."

The interview was Wednesday after school. To prepare, Michael did what he did before every challenge, which was nothing, on the theory that preparation desensitized you to spontaneity and spontaneity was his strength. This theory had survived a failed algebra quiz, a collapsed science project, and one disastrous turn as the anchor of the four-by-four relay, and it survived now, right up until the manager, a woman with reading glasses on a chain, asked him to describe a time he had dealt with a difficult customer or difficult person generally, and Michael began talking and did not stop for what felt like a fiscal quarter.

He talked about his neighbor's dog, which was obstreperous, and about mowing lawns, and about a feud with his sister over the remote, and somewhere in the middle he realized the manager had stopped writing anything down and was looking at him the way you look at a microwave that keeps running after the timer ends. He went home without being asked a second question. The manager said they would call, in the voice of someone who intended never to call anyone again, about anything.

"It went well," Michael told Tanner at lunch the next day. "I dominated the conversation."

"You talked for six minutes about a dog," Tanner said. "I was in the parking lot. I could see through the window. At one point she checked her phone."

"She was taking notes on her phone."

"She scrolled."

Anthony leaned across the table with his sandwich. Anthony had an actual job, at the hardware store, and wore this fact the way other people wore letter jackets. "You need the STAR method," he said. "That's what my manager told me when she hired me. Situation, Task, Action, Result. You tell it like a story that ends with what actually happened. Not a story that ends when you run out of air."

Michael said that sounded like something for people who couldn't improvise, and Anthony said Michael couldn't improvise, and Tanner pointed out that the evidence supported Anthony, and Michael ate his fries in the dignified silence of a man surrounded by fools.

But that night, in his room, he tried it anyway, mostly to prove it was unnecessary. He took the dog question. The situation: his neighbor's retriever had a nemesis, a tabby cat three doors down, and their battles regularly ended up in his yard. The task: get the dog home before it destroyed the Hendersons' begonias again without getting bitten. The action: he'd started carrying the dog's favorite ball on his walk home from school, so instead of chasing the cat he would chase the ball, all the way to his own porch. The result: two months, no begonia incidents, and the neighbor paid him ten dollars a week to keep it up. It was, he noticed, a story that took forty seconds instead of six minutes, and it ended somewhere instead of everywhere.

He was honest enough with himself, in the dark, to admit that this was a small blow to his worldview. He had always believed that being ready was for people with nothing interesting to say. Now it seemed possible that knowing where a story ended was itself a kind of interesting thing, and that structure wasn't the opposite of spontaneity but its container, like how a glass doesn't ruin water. He didn't like the thought, and he kept it anyway, the way you keep a rain jacket you resent needing.

On Friday he applied at the movie theater, the garden center, and the ice cream place by the bus loop. At the garden center the owner, a squat man named Mr. Becker who taught horticulture at the vocational school two towns over, asked him the customer question. Michael sat up straight, held the eye contact, and gave the dog and the ball and the ten dollars a week, Situation to Result, and watched Mr. Becker's pen actually move across the pad.

"Only trouble," Mr. Becker said, "is I don't have customers. I have plants, and plants don't chase cats. Tell me about a time you were responsible for something that could die because you forgot about it."

Michael opened his mouth, found nothing rehearsed living there, and closed it. Then he thought of the basil on his windowsill, which he had watered faithfully for three weeks and then neglected for five days while gaming, and which he had brought back from the edge with careful measuring and an apology he had felt ridiculous saying out loud. He started with the situation. He kept his eyes on Mr. Becker's, and behind the man's shoulder, through the greenhouse glass, the October light came down on rows of green things waiting for somebody responsible.

"So," Michael said, "do you want the part where it lives?"

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In translation, the ribosome moves along the messenger RNA and joins amino acids together with peptide bonds to build a protein chain.
story:
The retake was on Monday, and Luca had until then to understand the unit he had failed in June, which was why he was kneeling in the community garden on a Saturday morning with a biology textbook balanced on an upturned bucket. Ms. Cardinal, who ran the plots, had given him the bench near the tool shed on the condition that he help water the tomato rows before the sale. She said it without any real deterrence in her voice, the way his grandmother used to promise consequences she had no intention of enforcing, but Luca watered anyway, because the tomatoes were going brown at the shoulders and Bree had been caring for them all month.

Bree wanted the sale to cover the new fence, and she said so twice before nine o'clock. Her basil had failed, her peppers had been eaten by something unnamed, and the tomatoes were the last argument she had that the garden deserved its budget. She crouched across the row from Luca, pinching off yellowed leaves, and watched him stare at a diagram of a cell.

"You're supposed to be watering," she said.

"I am watering. I'm also dying." He turned the book so she could see the maze of arrows. "DNA gets copied into RNA, that part I get. Then the RNA goes out and something reads it and builds a protein. I can't hold it in my head at the same time as the first part."

Jameson arrived then, late, carrying a paper cup of coffee and the loose, unbothered walk of someone who had already passed biology with a C and considered the matter closed. He had come, he announced, because his mother wanted him out of the house, and because Bree had promised him free tomatoes. He sat on the bench, looked at Luca's book for exactly four seconds, and said, "My cousin explained that to me with beads once."

Luca was noncommittal, mostly because Jameson's explanations historically made things worse. But Jameson set his cup down, picked up a length of twine from the shed, and began threading cherry tomatoes onto it, one at a time, reading something invisible ahead of each one.

"Okay," Jameson said. "Say this string is the messenger RNA. It came out of the nucleus, it's the copy of the instructions. And say I'm the ribosome." He held his thumb and finger like a small mouth and slid them along the twine, picking up each tomato and pressing it against the last. "I move along it, and every three bases tell me one amino acid, and I join them together. Peptide bonds, that's the link. The whole string of amino acids is the protein." He lifted the strand, tomatoes swinging, red and irregular. "Protein chain."

Luca looked at the strand for a long moment. In the margin of his book the diagram had seemed to adumbrate something he couldn't name, a shadow of an idea without edges, and now the edges arrived. The ribosome wasn't a factory or a magic trick; it was a thumb and finger moving along a string, reading as it went, building as it read. "Wait," he said. "So the ribosome doesn't know what it's making. It just reads and joins, reads and joins."

"That's what my cousin said. It doesn't care. It's the order of the beads that makes the protein what it is."

Bree, who had been listening while she worked, held up a tomato she had just twisted from the vine. "So this is a protein chain that got folded up into a shape." She turned it in her fingers. "Instructions in the DNA, copied out, then strung together bead by bead, and then it becomes part of this."

"More or less," Luca said, and then, honestly, "I don't know the folding part yet. That's Monday's problem." He picked up the twine and slid his own thumb and finger along it, mouthing the sequence, and Jameson let him keep it, taking another from the shed to finish the row.

Ms. Cardinal came by near noon with a cash box and a folding table. She looked at the tomato strand still knotted at the end Luca had been holding, and at his book lying open in the dirt, and said nothing about either, only that the watering looked good and that if he wanted to keep the bench he should come back next Saturday. Bree counted the sale table's stock twice, calculating, and Luca heard her mutter a number that made her stand a little straighter.

On Sunday he made his own twine and bead version at the kitchen table, out of dried beans and thread, and quizzed himself until his mother told him to stop clicking the beans together. Monday morning, third period, the question on the retake asked exactly what the string had shown him, and he wrote it out fast, and after, walking out past the gym, he was already composing a text to Jameson, thumbs moving: tell your cousin thanks, and can she do folding.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: In 1936 the Literary Digest poll collected about 2.4 million responses yet predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt, who then won in a landslide.
story:
The poll appeared in the group chat at 11:47 on a Tuesday night, and by morning it had four hundred replies. Someone in Maya's grade had built a Google Form asking who should win the senior class presidency, and the numbers were lopsided: Angel trailed by nineteen points with two days of voting left. Maya read the thread on the bus, thumbing through message after message, most of them some version of "rip Angel" with a coffin emoji.

"It's over," Ryleigh typed from three seats behind her, and Maya turned around in time to see her grinning, phone held up like evidence. "Four hundred people, Maya. You can't argue with four hundred people."

Angel was slumped against the window in the seat across the aisle, headphones on, screen dark. He'd wanted this presidency for a year, had rehearsed his speech in the empty cafeteria until Ms. Clarke-Williams, doing lunch duty, told him the janitor thought a radio had been left on. Maya had watched all of it. She wanted to tell him the poll meant nothing, but she wasn't sure that was true, and she refused to externalize a confidence she didn't actually hold, not even to be kind.

In third period she typed a reply into the chat, deleted it, and typed a smaller one: "How did the poll get sent out?" Ryleigh answered with a shrugging emoji and a link. Maya clicked through and found the form had been posted in the robotics channel and the fantasy football channel and nowhere else. She sat with that for a moment, then opened her stats notes, because Ms. Clarke-Williams had spent exactly one October day on sampling and Maya had been half asleep through it.

The notes said almost nothing useful, so she searched on her phone during lunch, in the corner of the cafeteria where the wifi worked. She found a story from 1936: a magazine called the Literary Digest had run a poll and collected about 2.4 million responses, and it predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt. Roosevelt then won in a landslide. Maya read the sentence twice. Two point four million people, and the prediction had been exactly backwards.

She posted it to the chat: "In 1936 a poll got 2.4 million responses and said Landon would beat Roosevelt. Roosevelt won in a landslide." Then, after a breath: "Big numbers can still be wrong. Who the poll asks matters."

Ryleigh's reply came fast. "That's so anachronistic. This is a school poll, not 1936." Maya started to answer, then stopped, because Ryleigh had a point Maya couldn't dismiss: a robotics-channel sample wasn't obviously biased against Angel, who built drones in his garage. Maybe it was biased for him. She didn't know, and the honest version of her position had to include that not knowing. She closed the app and found Angel at his locker.

"Did you see what I posted?" she asked.

"I saw." He shut his locker. "Ryleigh says you're being romantic about it."

"Ryleigh thinks saying a number is just a number is nihilism. I think a number is just a number until you know who answered." Angel looked at her for a long second, and she could see him deciding whether to believe her, or whether to believe the four hundred, or whether both could be true at once and he'd still lose.

Voting closed Thursday at noon. At 12:15 the results were announced over the PA, and the cafeteria went quiet for the count: Angel by six votes, out of a senior class of two hundred and eleven. Ryleigh found Maya at the exit, phone out, the poll still open on her screen, the four hundred replies still predicting the other outcome with total certainty.

"So the poll was wrong," Ryleigh said.

"The poll was small and it asked the wrong rooms," Maya said. "Next time it could be right anyway. I'd still argue."

Ryleigh laughed once, short. "You'd argue with a landslide."

They walked out together, and behind them the cafeteria noise came up again like water filling a hole.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: North Dakota is the only US state without voter registration; it abolished registration in 1951, and voters instead show identification at the polls.
story:
The line at the community hall moved in small shuffles, the way lines do when everyone in them is being careful. Oliver had his driver's license in his hand before he reached the table, though nobody had asked for it yet, and he turned it over twice while he waited, reading his own address as if to confirm that he still lived there. Behind him, a woman was telling her husband which classroom the bake sale would be in. Ahead of him, a girl he half recognized from school, Eden, was standing at the check-in table with her hands flat on the surface, leaning forward, arguing in a polite and losing sort of way.

"I don't understand what you mean, register," Eden was saying. "I've voted before. You just show up."

The poll worker, patient, explained again that her name wasn't on the list, and that in this state you had to register in advance, and that unfortunately today was too late for that.

"But that's not how it works," Eden said. "That's not how it works anywhere. I'm from North Dakota. We don't have registration. North Dakota is the only state without it. They got rid of it in 1951. You just show your ID at the polls and they let you in."

Oliver, close enough now to hear all of this, felt something tilt in his head, the pleasant kind of tilt, like a door opening onto a room he hadn't known the house contained. He had never once thought about registration as a thing a state could simply not have. He had registered at the DMV six weeks ago, checking a box while also updating his organ donor status, and he had amortized the whole civic act across that errand, spread it thin, barely noticing it. And here was someone for whom the entire apparatus was foreign, standing at a folding table in a gymnasium that smelled of floor wax and coffee, unable to vote because of it.

"Wait," Oliver said, and then, because he hadn't planned to speak, he had to keep going. "You're saying you moved here from North Dakota and nobody told you that you had to register first?"

"Nobody told me there was a first," Eden said. "There's never been a first. You go, you show them who you are, you vote. My mom's voted in every election since before I was born and she has never registered for anything in her life."

The poll worker, to her credit, did not argue the point. She slid a pamphlet across the table and said the registration could be done online now, that it would take ten minutes, and that Eden would be set for November. Eden took the pamphlet the way you take a ticket for a train that has already left.

They ended up outside together, sitting on the concrete steps at the side of the hall, because Oliver had already voted and Eden had nothing else to do, and because there was a kind of obligation in having overheard the whole thing. She told him about Fargo, about how flat it was, how you could watch a storm come at you for an hour, and how the lake country in the northeast, the littoral scrub along Devil's Lake, was the only place the land folded at all. He told her he had never been anywhere flatter than the coastal plain two hours east, and she laughed and said that didn't count, that the ocean was its own kind of folding.

"Can I ask you something?" Oliver said. "Does it feel like a barrier, registering? Like they're making you prove something twice?"

Eden considered it, turning the pamphlet over in her hands. "I thought it would," she said. "When she said my name wasn't on the list, I felt like I'd been accused of something. But it's not that. It's more that I keep discovering the rules here one at a time, always after it's too late for that one."

He nodded, and found that his own opinion was not exactly an opinion yet, more a meeting of two thoughts that hadn't previously been introduced. He had always assumed registration was simply the price of admission, fair and unremarkable, the way his father assumed property taxes were the price of sidewalks. But if an entire state had run elections for seventy years without it, then the requirement wasn't a law of nature; it was a choice, one among possible choices, and choices could be asked about. He didn't know yet whether the choice was good. He suspected it was like most rules, defensible in a paragraph and shaky in a conversation, and he made a private note to have the conversation someday, with someone who knew more than a pamphlet.

"I was going to vote for the school bond," he offered, since he'd already done it and it seemed churlish to say so. "Or against it. I went back and forth for a week."

"What finally did it?"

"Honestly? I made a pro and con list and then ignored it and went with the thing that made me feel less like I was being talked into something. Which is probably casuistry, some fancy version of deciding first and justifying after."

"That's not casuistry," Eden said. "That's just being eighteen."

The doors opened behind them and the woman from the bake sale came out with a cardboard box of leftover coffee and paper cups, and she asked them if they wanted one, and they both said yes, and she poured, steam rising off the cups into the cold air while inside the hall the line moved forward by one more shuffle.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In a minor-key sonata-form movement, the exposition's second theme usually moves to the relative major, such as E-flat major in a movement in C minor.
story:
The garage smelled of cut grass and old gasoline, and Lily had spread the score of Mozart's C minor sonata across the hood of Ms. Zhu's retired station wagon because it was the only flat surface in the neighbourhood wide enough for it. She had a pencil behind each ear, one for marking and one for chewing, and Marc-Antoine kept stealing the chewing one.

"Exposition, development, recapitulation," Mathis said, reading off Lily's assignment sheet like a weather report. "It sounds like a legal firm."

"It sounds like three boxes," Lily said, "and I have to draw the lines where they start and stop. That's all Ms. Zhu wants. Brackets and labels."

"That's never all a teacher wants," Marc-Antoine said, and he was right, which was annoying of him.

She had done the easy part already. The first theme arrived immediately, stern and C minor, all commas and no questions. She put a bracket at the top of the page and wrote exposition in her neatest hand, the hand she saved for documents that would be inspected. The second theme, though, was the problem. She had a theory, formed at two in the morning and defended since breakfast with the conviction of the sleep-deprived: in a minor-key movement, the second theme would move to the dominant. She had even told Mathis so on the walk over, and Mathis, who inured himself to her theories the way one becomes inured to a dog that barks at every car, had only said "mm."

The garage door was open to the June evening, and the lilac by the driveway had gone fully arboreal over the spring, a small tree now rather than a bush, its shade lying across the third page of the score. Lily played the second theme on her phone, tinny through the speaker, then again through Marc-Antoine's better one, then a third time while following the notes. Something was not where she had promised it would be. The music had not gone where she expected; it had gone somewhere warmer, somewhere that felt like a room with the windows opened after a shut-in winter. She looked at the key signature on the page, looked again, and laughed out loud.

"Let me guess," Mathis said. "You were wrong and you're delighted about it."

"It's E-flat major," she said. "The second theme. I said it would go to the dominant, I told you that, and it doesn't, it goes to E-flat major. That's the relative major of C minor. It's a whole different plan than the one I made up." She wrote E-flat major above the second theme, then drew a little arrow, then, unable to help herself, crossed out her original guess in a way that left it legible, evidence of her own error preserved for the record.

Marc-Antoine leaned over the hood, frowning at the page as though it owed him a personal apology. "So how were you supposed to know that without, what, knowing the piece already?"

"You play it. You listen and you follow and the page tells you." She tapped the key signature with the chewed pencil, which Marc-Antoine had finally surrendered. "The rules aren't the rules until the piece shows you which rules it keeps."

"That's the most Lily sentence ever spoken," Mathis said. "You could frame it."

She kept working while the light went amber and the moths came in under the garage door, doing their moth errands against the bare bulb. Development bracket: yes, there, where the first theme got taken apart like an engine on a tarp, all its bolts in a row. Recapitulation: there, first theme back in C minor, stern again, commas again. But the second theme in the recapitulation sat in C minor's own warmth instead of E-flat, and she stopped over that for a long minute, pencil hovering, because she could hear the difference and could not yet say what it meant, only that the piece brought something home rather than leaving it where it had first been found.

Ms. Zhu came out with a tray of barley tea and set it on the fender. She looked at the score, at the brackets, at the crossed-out guess, and her face did something small and amused. "You went looking for the dominant," she said.

Lily felt her ears go hot. "How did you know?"

"Because I made the same guess at your age, in this garage, on this car, and my teacher let me write it down before he corrected me. He said the second theme of a minor-key movement usually moves to the relative major, and I never forgot it because he made me earn it first." Ms. Zhu poured three glasses, hers the fourth, and pointed at Lily's pencil. "The crossing-out stays. That's the best mark on the page."

Marc-Antoine raised his glass. "To being wrong in a nice garage."

Lily drank, set down the glass, and picked the pencil back up. Above the recapitulation's second theme she wrote, in small letters, asks a question I can't answer yet, and underlined it twice.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Paul Boyer and John Walker shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for explaining how ATP synthase makes ATP.
story:
Connor spread the flashcards across the picnic table in the backyard, weighting the corners with stones because the wind kept lifting them like it wanted to read them first. Glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain, oxidative phosphorylation. Mr. Trimble's biology exam was Thursday, and Connor had promised his mother he would know it cold by Wednesday night, which was a way of promising himself, since she would never check.

The problem was that he did not actually understand it. He could recite the sequence the way he could recite the lyrics of songs he didn't like, but if anyone asked him why glucose ended up as ATP, or what the mitochondria were actually doing in there, he had nothing. It was like knowing the names of a town's streets without a map.

Kalen came through the gate first, holding a bag of cherries, and Hugh followed with his laptop under his arm because Hugh brought his laptop everywhere, the way other people brought their anxieties. They sat down on either side of the cards and began quizzing him, and Connor began to fail, quietly and thoroughly. He mixed up where the electron carriers loaded and unloaded. He said the mitochondria made ATP in glycolysis, and Kalen winced.

"Okay, stop," Hugh said. "My dad says memorizing without a model is the most pernicious habit in studying. You think you know it, so you stop looking."

"Your dad says a lot," Kalen said, but he was already sorting the cards into a line on the table, glucose at one end, ATP at the other.

Connor opened the laptop himself and typed in ATP synthase, because that was the one term that had refused to stick all week. The first result was an image of the enzyme, and it looked like a mushroom with a stalk and a spinning head, like something from a machine shop rather than a cell. He read the caption twice. Below it, in smaller type, was a sentence about Paul Boyer and John Walker, who had shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for explaining how ATP synthase makes ATP.

He read it aloud. "They gave a Nobel Prize for one enzyme."

"Two people, one enzyme," Kalen said, spitting a cherry pit into the grass.

Connor sat back. All week he had been treating the pathway like a list of chores, and it turned out that one step in the list, a single protein turning in a membrane, had taken two careers to figure out. Something about that reorganized the whole subject in his head. It wasn't a chore list. It was a machine that people had spent their lives disassembling in the dark.

Mr. Watanabe appeared at the fence then, watering can in hand, his tomato plants leaning toward the conversation the way tomato plants lean toward anything. He asked what they were studying, and Connor told him, expecting the polite nod adults gave to teenage preoccupations. Instead Mr. Watanabe set down the watering can and asked whether they had reached the part where the enzyme rotates. When Connor said they had, the old man said, "In my first year of university, that was still an argument. Nobody could say how it worked. Then Boyer and Walker worked it out, and it earned them the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry." He picked up his watering can, watered the tomatoes, and went back inside his own yard, leaving the three of them staring after him.

"I didn't know he did science," Hugh said.

"Nobody imputes anything to that man," Kalen said. "He could be a retired spy."

Connor looked down the line of cards again. He thought about how, in history class, they had spent a week on historiography, on how the story of a thing changes depending on who is telling it, and he had liked that because it meant knowledge had a shape you could see. He had assumed biology was different, that it was just facts sitting there like coins in a drawer. But here was the same shape: a question nobody could answer, then two people in two different countries answering it, then a prize, then a diagram on a website, then a retired man at a fence remembering when it was still an argument. The diagram was the end of a story, not the absence of one.

He still could not explain oxidative phosphorylation, not really. He knew that much about himself now, and it was an honest kind of knowing. He picked up the card for the transport chain, then the card for ATP synthase, and placed them side by side at the end of the line. "Quiz me again," he said. "But this time ask me why."

Kalen shuffled the deck. Hugh turned the laptop so the spinning enzyme faced them all, its little mushroom head caught mid-rotation, and Connor leaned in.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Starting with applicants for 2026 entry, UCAS replaced the free-form personal statement with three structured questions about why the applicant wants the subject and how they have prepared.
story:
Christopher had claimed the corner table by the window of the coffee shop because it had the only outlet that worked, and because from there he could watch the door. He had his laptop open, his cousin's email printed and folded beside the mug, and forty minutes before the admissions portal updated. Three months of work and one essay, or what he had believed was one essay, were about to be judged.

"You're doing the thing," Kelsey said, setting down her latte without sitting. "The refresh thing. You've refreshed it twice since I walked over."

"It updates at noon. It's eleven fifty."

Nina dropped into the chair across from him and stole the printed email without asking. She read it the way she read everything, fast and out loud in her head, her lips moving slightly. "Your cousin says write a personal statement that tells a story. Arc. Hook. Something about not starting with a quote."

"That's the advice. He got into Edinburgh with it, so it works."

Nina turned the page over, then back, frowning at the header. "When did he apply?"

"Two years ago. Why?"

"Because this is the wrong shape." She tapped the screen of her own phone, thumbed through something, and slid it across to him. "Look. Starting with applicants for 2026 entry, UCAS replaced the free-form personal statement with three structured questions. One on why you want the subject, one on how you've prepared. There's a third one too."

Christopher looked at the screen. The words rearranged themselves in his stomach. His essay, the essay he had already submitted, the essay with the hook about his grandfather's shed and the paragraph of scene-setting his cousin had insisted on, was built for a form that no longer existed. He had written a story when they had asked, three times, for reasons.

"That can't be right," he said, but he was already scrolling, and it was right, and the form he remembered filling in last autumn suddenly looked different in his memory, boxes where he had pictured open field. He had pasted his beautiful intro into the first box because it felt like a beginning, and he had never once asked what the box was for. His cousin's advice wasn't wrong. It was just advice from a country he no longer lived in, an antiquated map of a road that had been rebuilt.

"Wait," Nina said. "You submitted in October. It's March. Why are you spiralling now?"

"Because the answer comes at noon."

"So the spiralling is decorative," Kelsey said, and finally sat down.

Mr. Friedman, who owned the place and had been wiping the counter since before any of them were born, came over with a cloth and no intention of leaving. "You three want more room in those cups, or is this a vigil?"

"Vigil," Nina said.

He refilled Christopher's mug anyway, unasked, and stood there with the pot held low, an old habit from a man who liked to circumscribe his kindness with small practical gestures so it wouldn't be mistaken for something that needed acknowledging. Steam rose between them. Christopher closed the laptop, which surprised him, and told them the whole thing, the shed, the hook, the boxes, the map that no longer matched the territory.

"Here's what I keep going back and forth on," he said. "Part of me thinks the three questions are better. They tell you exactly what they want, so you can't waste your shot on atmosphere. No encumbrance, just evidence. But part of me thinks my cousin's way was doing something real, that a person reading five thousand applications remembers a story and forgets a list of reasons. I don't know which of those is true. Maybe the story only works if you're already the kind of applicant they want, and the questions just make you prove it earlier."

"So which do you believe?" Nina asked.

"Both, a little. I think the questions are fairer and the essay was better writing, and I submitted worse writing because I didn't check what year it was." He laughed once, without much in it. "That's not a position, exactly. It's more like a coin I can't stop turning over."

The clock over the pastry case said 11:59. Kelsey reached across and closed the lid of his laptop, which was already closed, so she just rested her hand on it, which somehow meant steady. Nina turned his phone face down beside the sugar. Mr. Friedman went back to the counter and began grinding coffee, loudly, deliberately, the way a man does when he is giving a room something else to listen to.

At 12:01 the phone buzzed against the table, twice, insistently, and all three of them looked at it lying there in its own small shadow. Christopher picked it up, thumbed in the passcode wrong once, right the second time, and read. His face did nothing for a long second, and then everything.

"Well?" Kelsey said.

He turned the screen toward them. "It's conditional on the Physics. Which I already have. Which means, I think, it means."

"Say it," Nina said.

He was still holding the phone up, the steam from the mug drifting between him and the words, when he said, "I got in. I actually got in."

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: Andrew Wakefield's 1998 paper in The Lancet claiming a link between the MMR vaccine and autism was based on only twelve children.
story:
Ethan spread the two articles across his grandmother's kitchen table, weighting the corners with salt shakers because the window was open and the October wind kept lifting the pages. The assignment was due Monday: a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question, and the question his teacher had approved was whether the MMR vaccine was linked to autism. One article was a study published in The Lancet in 1998, claiming a link. The other was a large epidemiological study from years later that found no link at all. Ethan had read each twice and still had nothing on his laptop but a title and his name.

He had come to his grandmother's house for the weekend because his own house had three younger siblings and no quiet, and because his grandfather kept a study off the back hallway with a desk lamp that worked and a door that closed. His grandfather was at the table too, sorting through papers from the bank, a disbursement notice from his pension fund and a letter about property tax, and he glanced at Ethan's pages without comment for most of the morning.

At noon Liberty texted him a photo of her own draft, six pages already, and a message that said she'd found twelve points of comparison. Noa texted half an hour later asking whether Ethan wanted to meet at the library on Sunday, and Ethan typed back that he was at his grandparents' and might not finish at all. He set the phone face down on the table.

The trouble, as far as Ethan could name it, was that the two articles seemed to be doing different things entirely. The Lancet paper described children, cases, histories, what the paper called an affective sense of alarm in the parents' accounts. The later study was mostly tables, populations, statistical rates across whole countries. He could describe the difference. What he could not yet do was say which difference mattered, or why one article's evidence should count for more, and his English teacher had written at the bottom of his outline, "Comparison is not a list. Take a position."

He read the methods section of the Lancet paper again, slowly, with a pencil. Somewhere in the middle of it he stopped and counted. The study described twelve children. He counted again, marking each case with a small tick. Twelve. He sat back. He turned to the later study and found its number, and the number was in the hundreds of thousands, and he sat with both figures side by side on a scrap of paper because the difference was so large it looked almost like a typo.

"Twelve," he said out loud, mostly to himself.

"Twelve what?" his grandfather asked, not looking up from the tax letter.

"Kids. In one of these studies. It's based on only twelve children." Ethan turned the scrap paper toward him. "The other one looked at hundreds of thousands. Same question."

His grandfather put down his pen. He came around the table and read both numbers, tapping each with one finger. "You can't build much of a bridge on twelve pilings," he said. He was a retired surveyor and spoke like one. "Doesn't absolve the other paper, mind you. A big study can be built badly too. But you check the footing before you check the paint."

That afternoon Ethan walked the two blocks to the hardware store to buy a new printer cartridge, because his grandmother's printer had died mid-page on a draft and she had insisted. On the way back Mr. Jean-Louis, who taught chemistry at the community college and lived three doors down, was raking leaves in his yard, and Ethan stopped at the fence because Mr. Jean-Louis had once told him to stop by if physics homework ever defeated him.

"I'm writing a review of two articles," Ethan said. "One of them is that 1998 Lancet paper. The one that claimed the vaccine was linked to autism." Mr. Jean-Louis stopped raking. Ethan showed him the scrap of paper with the two numbers. "Twelve children in that study. The other one's a huge population study, and it found nothing."

"Which one do you believe?" Mr. Jean-Louis asked.

Ethan said he didn't think it was about believing, exactly, and then heard how that sounded, and tried again. "I think the small one can show you a question worth asking. It can't really answer it. The big one tries to answer it." He paused. "But the big one is about rates and populations, and it doesn't tell you anything about a single kid. So I still don't know how you'd know for one specific kid."

Mr. Jean-Louis picked up the rake again. "Then say that," he said. "Say exactly that. The honest review is the one that says here is what we know and here is where the knowing stops."

Back in the study, Ethan opened his laptop and deleted his old title. He wrote for two hours while his grandmother cooked something with onions, and what he wrote went like this: that the two articles were not merely disagreeing but operating at different scales, that a study of twelve children could generate a hypothesis and a public panic but could not carry the weight of a general claim, and that the population study answered the general claim and left the individual case, the one worried parent in one waiting room, outside its reach. He wrote a paragraph acknowledging what stayed uncertain for him, whether small careful studies had a value that numbers alone could not replace, and he let the paragraph end on the question rather than resolving it. When his grandfather came in to say dinner was ready, Ethan was still typing. "Save it and come eat," his grandfather said, and Ethan hit save, and closed the laptop on the tick marks.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: In the United States, every new employee must complete Section 1 of Form I-9, which verifies identity and permission to work, no later than their first day of paid work.
story:
The hardware store smelled of cut pine and machine oil, and Robert stood at the register counter with a clipboard in his hands, reading the same line four times without taking it in. He had been hired on Tuesday, over the phone, by a man named Mr. Georgiou who owned the place, and he had walked the eleven blocks that Saturday morning believing his first task would be learning where the lag bolts were kept. Instead there was paperwork, and the paperwork was asking him things he had never been asked before.

"You look like a man reviewing a mortgage," said Rebecca, who was already in the red store apron, restocking tape measures two aisles over. They had chem together at school. She had told him about the opening in the first place, which made the clipboard feel less like an ambush and more like a test she had already passed.

"It's a form I've never seen before," Robert said. "It wants me to certify that I'm a citizen or national or lawful permanent resident. It has three boxes. If I check one, I swear it's true under penalty of perjury." He said the last part quietly, the way people repeat legal language, as if the words might bruise.

"That's Section 1 of the I-9," Rebecca said. "Everybody does one."

Mr. Georgiou came out from behind the paint counter, wiping his hands on a rag, and set a jar of pens in front of Robert as if it were an offering. He did not launch into any explanation. He said only, "You can't start paid work until that's done. It has to be finished no later than your first day. Today is your first day, so." He lifted one shoulder and went back to tinting a gallon of eggshell for a woman waiting by the fan decks.

Robert checked the first box, printed his name, and read the date line twice before committing his signature to it. Then came the part that unsettled him: he was supposed to have brought a document, a passport or a birth certificate or something, and he had brought nothing but his phone, his house key, and a laminated card from the pool where he'd lifeguarded one summer, unpaid, for his father's friend. The pool card proved he could swim, not that he existed.

He stepped outside to call his mother. The morning was already warm, and a delivery truck idled at the curb with its hazard lights ticking. She answered on the third ring, and when he explained, he could hear her moving through the kitchen, a drawer opening, the small percussion of a house being searched.
