"I'll bring your birth certificate," she said. "It's in the fire box. I can be there by noon." He felt the strange double weight of the call: pride at being adult enough to have this problem, and embarrassment at needing to be rescued from it. His father had a theory that hardship built character, that a boy should sublimate every discomfort into effort, and Robert had spent years half believing it and half suspecting it was an affectation, a philosophy worn like a hat. Right now, standing in the sun with an unfinished form inside, he suspected it more than half.

Back in the store, he decided not to stand idle until noon. He found Mr. Georgiou and asked whether there was anything he could do while he waited that wasn't paid work, and the man studied him for a moment with the rag over his shoulder. "You can learn the aisles," Mr. Georgiou said. "Looking is free." So Robert spent the next two hours wandering the store with Rebecca, who had stopped pretending to restock and was walking him through the layout instead. She knew everything. The difference between a machine bolt and a carriage bolt. Which hinges squeaked and which didn't. Where the good work gloves hid because customers bought the cheap ones first.

"The cheap ones are almost the same," she said, handing him a pair to feel. "The expensive ones are only better if you're going to wear them every day for years. Otherwise it's just gratuitous. Like paying eight dollars for water."

"Elianne would disagree," Robert said, naming their classmate, who bought the expensive version of everything and defended it with charts. Rebecca laughed, a short real laugh, and a man in the next aisle looked over and then smiled despite himself.

At quarter past twelve his mother came through the door with the birth certificate in a manila envelope, slightly bent from her bag, and Robert signed the remaining line while Mr. Georgiou watched without hovering. The man looked at the document, made a small note in his own ledger, and handed the certificate back as though returning something borrowed, which, Robert thought, was exactly what it was.

"So I'm official," Robert said.

"You started two hours ago," Mr. Georgiou said. "You just didn't get paid for it." He handed Robert a red apron, folded into a square. Robert shook it out and put it on over his head, and the strap caught on his ear, and Rebecca reached over and straightened it without comment. Then he turned down aisle seven, where a woman in paint-spattered shoes was holding up two nearly identical pieces of sandpaper, looking back and forth between them like a judge.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: The Islamic calendar is lunar and about 10 to 11 days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr come roughly 10 to 11 days earlier each year.
story:
The parking lot behind the masjid had been transformed overnight into something between a market and a party, and Camille stood at the edge of it with a tray of dates she was supposed to be carrying to the dessert table. Last Eid she had not been here at all. She had been three states away at a soccer showcase, telling herself that Eid would come around again next summer, and her mother had said fine, fine, go, in a voice that made it clear it was not fine. That had been twelve months ago, and she had carried the decision around ever since, the way you carry a stone in a coat pocket, forgetting it and then finding it with your hand.

"Camille, the dates," her aunt called, and Camille moved.

Caylee arrived around noon, wearing the green scarf she'd bought at last year's festival, back when Camille had still been the kind of person who went to the festival. Caylee had come that year as a guest, wide-eyed at the food stalls, and had returned this year on her own, which Camille found quietly remarkable. They walked the rows together. Caylee stopped at a stall selling embroidered bracelets, three for five dollars, and pointed across the lot at another stall selling nearly identical ones for four dollars each.

"This is arbitrage," Caylee said, holding up a bracelet. "We buy them here, sell them over there to people who didn't walk this far, and we clear, like, a dollar a bracelet."

"That's not arbitrage, that's annoying strangers."

"It's commerce. It's grandiose commerce. I'm building an empire on a church parking lot."

"Masjid," Camille said, but she was smiling, and for a minute the stone in her pocket felt lighter.

The trouble came later, at the information table, where a laminated schedule listed the youth halaqa, the Qur'an recitation, and, in bold at the bottom, a notice about Eid falling during exam week this year. Camille stared at it. Last year Eid had been in the summer, full stop, a green field and a showcase jersey. She had built her plan for this year on that assumption: that Eid would stay put, that she could compartmentalize it the way she compartmentalized everything, school in one box, family in another, opened on schedule. Her mother was already saying something about which day they would cook, and Camille heard herself ask, out loud, why it was different this year.

Mr. Cruz, who taught chemistry at the high school and lived four houses down and had come, he said, because the food was unbeatable, was standing near the table holding a plate of samosas. He asked the same question before she could take it back. "Doesn't it always land around the same time? I thought it was a summer thing."

"It's a lunar calendar," Camille said, and then heard the rest come out of her, a sentence she hadn't known she owned. "It's about ten to eleven days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan and Eid come roughly ten to eleven days earlier every year." She had learned it somewhere, probably from her grandmother, years ago, and had filed it away without ever once using it to check her own plans. It had been in summer last year and the summer before that because it had been drifting backward through the calendar all along, and she had been drifting forward on the assumption that nothing moved.

"So next year it's even earlier," Caylee said slowly, working it through. "And the year after that, earlier still. It never stops?"

"It never stops."

Mr. Cruz whistled and said something about his lesson planning, that he had a student last spring who had been stunned to find Eid sitting in the middle of finals, and Camille nodded and did not say that she understood that student completely now. She was thinking about the stone in her pocket. She had told herself the showcase was a one-time choice, a single trade, family for a shot at being seen by a scout, and that the trade could be balanced later. But there was no fixed later. The calendar kept moving, and every choice she made against it was made against a moving target, and the scout had never called, and her mother's voice on that phone call a year ago had never stopped being not fine.

Her mother found her by the dessert table, sorting dates onto a platter, and stood beside her without saying anything for a while. The lot was loud with kids racing between the game booths, and someone's speaker was playing a nasheed turned up too loud, and the afternoon light was going amber over the tops of the tents.

"I can help with the morning," Camille said. "The cooking, I mean. Before exams. I already looked at the schedule." She had not looked at anything yet, actually, but she would, tonight, with the bold-print notice folded in her pocket next to the stone. She still didn't know whether she was making up for last year or just refusing to repeat it, and she was honest enough with herself to leave that question open. What she knew was smaller and firmer: the date would not hold still, so neither could she.

Her mother picked up a date, considered it, and put it back on the platter, crooked.

"Start with the tea," her mother said. "The cardamom's in the trunk."

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: In many tax systems, a deduction lowers the income that tax is calculated on, while a tax credit subtracts directly from the tax owed, so a credit is usually worth more than an equal deduction.
story:
The waiting room of Virtanen Accounting smelled of toner and old coffee, and every chair was full because it was the last day to file. Aiden had taken the day off from the hardware store, and in his backpack he carried a shoebox: eleven paycheque stubs, a folder of receipts, and a tuition slip he'd been afraid to open. Mr. Virtanen had agreed to squeeze him in at noon, between two farmers and a woman who kept checking her watch. Mariah sat beside him with her own folder on her knees, because she'd missed her bus and he'd offered her the ride, and because she was trying not to look like she was panicking.

"I only need one question answered," she said, turning her phone over and over. "Whether my textbooks count. I don't want to pay for a whole appointment for one question."

"Then ask it while he does mine," Aiden said. "It's not like he's going to bill you for sitting in a chair."

She gave him a look that said she suspected the world did, in fact, bill you for sitting in chairs, and then her name was called from the front desk, and a minute later his was.

Mr. Virtanen's office was small and windowless, papered in file folders. He was older than Aiden expected, with reading glasses pushed up on his forehead, and he waved them both in without ceremony. "First return?" he asked, and when Aiden nodded, he said, "Good. Everyone should do their first one on paper, at least once, so they know what the machine is doing to them." He spread the paycheque stubs across the desk like cards and tapped one with two fingers. "See this line. That's income tax taken off at the source. This one, that's your pension contribution. Notice what's left at the bottom, and notice that the sales tax you paid at the store isn't anywhere on here. That's a different animal entirely, and it lives on your receipts."

Aiden laid out the receipts. There were coffee ones, a bus pass, a soldering iron for a class project, and the thick tuition slip, which had transfixed him when it arrived in February: the number at the bottom had seemed too large to be about him, something a bank would own. Mr. Virtanen entered the figures steadily, and Mariah, still standing by the door, held out her textbook receipts without being asked. He took them without comment and stacked them beside Aiden's tuition slip.

"Here's where it gets interesting," Mr. Virtanen said, and turned the monitor so they could both see. "Your tuition and these receipts, they go here. That's a deduction. It lowers the income your tax is calculated on." He moved the cursor. "But this line, from your tuition slip as well, that's a credit. It subtracts directly from the tax you owe." He said it plainly, as a man reading a label off a jar, and then he leaned back and let them look.

Mariah got there first. She was staring at the two lines, and then she said, "Wait. So if they're the same amount, the credit's worth more. It comes off at the end, after everything's already been calculated."

"That's the shape of it," Mr. Virtanen said, and went back to typing.

Aiden sat with it, watching the numbers rearrange themselves as the program recalculated. He had come in with a theory, one Trystan had handed him at lunch last week: that deductions were where the real money was, that credits were for people who didn't know better. Trystan had filed with an app and a shrug, and his refund had sounded enormous, and Aiden had half believed him and half suspected him of making the whole thing up. Now the screen was showing him something quieter and stranger, that the two things were not rivals but ran on different tracks entirely, and that a person could hold both ideas at once the way a river holds two currents. He thought of it almost as a symbiosis, the system working because the parts worked on each other, though he wasn't sure the word fit and wasn't sure it mattered that he wasn't sure.

"What about hers?" Aiden asked, nodding at Mariah's textbooks. "Same thing?"

"Different province, different slip," Mr. Virtanen said. "Yours carries the credit forward. Hers may not." He printed a page for her, one page, and slid it across the desk, and pointed at a box with his pen. "That's your answer, for whatever it costs you, which today is nothing." Mariah folded the page like it was a letter from someone she'd been waiting to hear from.

When they were back in the hallway, the clock over the front desk said twelve-forty, and the waiting room had only gotten fuller. Mariah held the page against her chest. "I can get my refund," she said. "I was going to use it for the deposit on the apartment. If I'd missed today I'd have lost the whole summer to my mother's couch."

Aiden signed his forms at the front desk, paid in cash from the shoebox's last envelope, and pocketed the receipt with the sales tax printed neatly at the bottom, one small line among others. He still didn't know whether Trystan had been lying or lucky, and he still didn't understand why the system was built with two doors instead of one, only that he'd walked through both today and come out holding a cheque for money he'd already earned once. Outside, Mariah was already on her phone, saying, "Mom, I'm coming by, don't start dinner," and Aiden held the door for a man carrying three boxes of receipts, who nodded at him like they were the last two sober people at a party.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: A plagal cadence moves from the IV chord to the I chord and is often called the 'Amen cadence' because many hymns sing 'Amen' to it.
story:
The community centre had one piano that stayed unlocked, an upright with a chip in the middle C, and Mr. Cruz let Gabriella use it on Thursday evenings after the seniors' bingo cleared out. Her assignment was due Monday: sixteen bars, melody with chord changes, written out in standard notation, her first real attempt at composing anything longer than the eight-bar exercises she had dashed off all term. She had eleven bars that she liked and five that she hated, and the hated ones were the ending.

The trouble was the ending. Her melody closed on the tonic, but the chord underneath wanted to go somewhere else first, and she couldn't hear where. She played the phrase four times, and four times it landed like a door shutting on her fingers.

Sabrina appeared in the doorway with two bags of chips from the vending machine, headphones hanging around her neck. "You're still on the same four bars," she said, dropping onto the folding chair beside the bench. "It's been twenty minutes."

"I heard you from the hallway," Cedrik said behind her, and he leaned on the piano's lid, where he was not supposed to lean. "It's the last chord. Everything before it is fine. You go somewhere and then you just, stop."

Gabriella knew he was right, which was annoying, because Cedrik had a way of being right about her music that had ossified over the years into something she relied on and resented in equal measure. Since middle school he had been the one who could hear the wrong note in a whole band rehearsal. "I need a chord before the final one," she said. "Something that makes the last chord feel finished. I just don't know what it is."

"Try the four chord," Cedrik said. "In the key of C, F. Then go to C."

She played it: F, then C, the melody floating down to its resting note over the change. Something opened and then settled. She played it again. "That's it. What is that?"

Sabrina had gone still, one chip halfway to her mouth. "My grandma does that. At the end of hymns. She hums it after the last line, the Amen part. It goes like that, exactly like that." She sang a soft two-syllable "A-men" over the chords as Gabriella played them again, and it fit, absurdly, perfectly.

"Amen cadence," Cedrik said. "That's what it's called. It goes from the four chord to the one." He shrugged. "I read ahead in the workbook."

Gabriella looked at her own handwritten pages, the eleven bars she had guarded all week, and felt something she couldn't quite name. Her grandmother had died two springs ago, before Gabriella had started theory, and the grandmother had hummed through whole Sunday services, never once calling it anything. All those Amens, and Gabriella had thought of them as decoration, an old woman's habit, when they had been the same material she was now sweating over on a Thursday night. It made her feel like an egoist, briefly, as though she had believed music only existed once she had learned its names.

She wrote the chords into her pages, F to C, and drew the final barline. Then she played the sixteen bars through from the top, slower than tempo, and Sabrina hummed the Amen under the last two chords without being asked, and Cedrik tapped the beat on the piano lid with two fingers, which he was still not supposed to do.

"It's not really finished," Gabriella said when the sound had gone. "It works, but I don't know if it's mine. The ending is a thing that already exists everywhere. Hymns, grandma, the workbook."

"So is every chord," Sabrina said. "Nobody invented C major either."

"I know. But it feels like I borrowed the part that matters most." Gabriella pulled the pages toward her and looked at bar fifteen, the F chord sitting there in her own cramped notation, half notes and stems pointing the wrong way. She thought about how her grandmother had never written anything down, how the music had passed through her and out of her without ever being possessed, and how that was either a kind of freedom or a kind of loss. The summer had felt metamorphic in that way, everything she'd known rearranging itself into new shapes, and she couldn't tell yet which of the shapes would last into the fall, when she'd be in a classroom three hundred miles from this piano.

Mr. Cruz put his head in at the end of the corridor, keys jangling, the signal that the building was closing. Gabriella gathered her pages, and Sabrina crumpled the empty chip bags, and Cedrik held the door.

"Play it once more before Monday," Cedrik said. "The ending's good."

"It's borrowed," Gabriella said.

"It's a plagal cadence," he said. "It's everyone's."

She laughed, folded the pages in half, and slid them into her backpack between a water bottle and a college housing form she still hadn't mailed. Outside, the parking lot lights were just coming on, and Sabrina was already humming the last two chords again, softly, like she was taking them home too.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Robert Cialdini's 1976 study found that students wore more university clothing after their football team won and said 'we' more when describing wins than losses.
story:
The stadium smelled like burnt pretzels and rain that hadn't fallen yet, and Blake had been holding the same napkin, shredded into a small white flower, since the second quarter. His mother sat on his left, explaining penalties to nobody. On his right, Veronika leaned forward with her elbows on her knees, watching the field the way some people watch a pot that refuses to boil.

The home team was down by four with six minutes left, and the whole lower bowl had contracted into a single nervous organism. When the quarterback scrambled for a first down, forty thousand strangers touched one another, and Blake noticed that he had grabbed Veronika's sleeve without deciding to. He let go. She hadn't seemed to mind, or hadn't noticed, which was somehow a different thing, and he filed the difference away the way he filed most things, in a mental drawer that his ex-stepfather had once called the drawer of stuff nobody asked about.

He had brought the drawer with him to the stadium, because before the game, in the parking lot, Maryam had been reading his psychology paper out loud to tease him. Robert Cialdini, 1976, she'd recited, in her game-show announcer voice. Students wore more of the university's clothing after the football team won. They said "we" more describing wins than losses. Maryam had waved the paper like a subpoena. That's your big finding? People like winning?

Blake had tried to explain that it wasn't about liking winning, it was about the pronoun, the little word people borrowed from strangers in helmets. He hadn't explained it well. Maryam had taken a bite of his sandwich as payment for listening, which was her standard rate, and Mr. Liu, whose season tickets were three rows ahead and who had come over to say hello to Blake's mother, had smiled at the argument the way adults smile at a card game they remember playing.

Now the clock ran under two minutes and the home team had the ball on the opponent's thirty. The crowd noise stopped being sound and became pressure, a physical thing against the eardrums. Blake watched his mother stand up, this woman who called football "the hitting show," and scream at a man she would never meet to throw the ball. He watched himself watch her. That was his real problem, his sister used to say, that he was always standing slightly outside the window of his own life, taking notes.

He tested it. Quietly, in his head, he tried the sentence both ways, and there was no hiding from the result. When the receiver dropped a pass in the end zone, his inner voice said they blew it, they can't finish. When the next play went for a touchdown, the voice said without hesitation, we did it, we needed that. Same mouth, same distance from the field, and the pronoun had switched sides like a free agent. He laughed out loud, a small strange laugh, and Veronika turned.

"What," she said, not really asking.

"Nothing. I'm an experiment."

"You're a what?"

The extra point went through, and the place detonated. Maryam, who had spent four quarters announcing that she didn't care about sports, who had never once worn anything with the university's name on it, was on her chair with her fists over her head, wearing his spare scarf, the one with the school colors, because her jacket had been cold. WE WON, she screamed at the section, at the sky, WE WON. She had never played a down in her life. Blake pointed at her and looked at Veronika with the expression of a man presenting evidence.

"Say that again," he said.

"We won," Maryam said, glowing, and then, catching his face, "What? Why are you being creepy?"

He told them, shouting a little over the noise. The study, the year, the clothing counts after wins, the we that showed up for victories and thinned out for losses like a fair-weather friend. He kept it short because the crowd kept interrupting itself with chants. Veronika listened with her chin propped on her hand, which was either attention or the prelude to a demolition, and he couldn't tell which, and that uncertainty sat comfortably beside all the others.

"So I'm a lab rat," Maryam said. "Thanks. Next time we lose, I'll say they lost, is that the finding? That I'm a charlatan about my own cheering?"

"It's not fake," Blake said. "That's the part I got wrong before. I thought it was a scam people ran on themselves. But it doesn't feel like a scam from inside. It feels like being part of something." He hesitated, because he could feel the two ideas refusing to sit in the same chair. "Maybe both are true. You didn't do anything, and you're still in it. I can't make those fit together yet."

"That's the most you thing you've ever said," Veronika said, but not unkindly. She pulled the scarf loose from Maryam's neck and held it up, turning it in the stadium light, examining it like a piece of evidence. "So if I put this on right now, am I joining, or am I just cold?"

Blake started to answer, found that he had two answers, and watched her wrap it twice around her own throat and face the field, where the players were kneeling out the clock and confetti cannons were being wheeled to the hash marks.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In Texas v. Johnson (1989), the Supreme Court ruled 5-4 that burning the American flag as a political protest is protected symbolic speech.
story:
The courthouse smelled of floor wax and old paper, and the marble stairs rang under Anthony's dress shoes, shoes he had borrowed from his father and that pinched at the heel. In the second-floor courtroom, where the real judges sat on weekdays, folding tables had been set up for the mock court, and Mr. Oyelaran was already at the bench in his gray suit, arranging index cards like a man dealing himself a hand of solitaire.

Anthony had drawn the wrong side. That was how he thought of it, anyway, on the bus that morning and for three nights before that: he was assigned to argue against Gregory Lee Johnson, against the man who had burned an American flag outside the 1984 Republican convention and then walked away with the Supreme Court's blessing. Trista had the other side, the easy side, and she kept telling him so in the hallway outside chemistry. "All I have to do is stand there and quote the majority," she had said. "You have to make burning a flag into a crime with a straight face."

He had tried. His first draft was a rant about veterans and soldiers' graves, and when he read it aloud in his bedroom his own voice embarrassed him. It imputed dishonor to people who had never said they felt dishonored, and he knew it. His mother, drying a pot at the sink, had listened to one paragraph and said only, "Is that what you believe, or what you think you're supposed to say?" He hadn't answered, because the honest answer was neither.

The turn had come Tuesday night in the library, in the orange light of the microfiche room no one used anymore, when Antony slid a photocopied page across the table and tapped one line with two fingers. "Look at the vote," Antony said. "Five to four." Anthony read it twice. Texas v. Johnson, 1989: the Supreme Court had ruled, five justices to four, that burning the flag as political protest was protected symbolic speech. Five to four. The margin of one bored juror, one traffic jam, one changed mind. The case Anthony had been treating like a wall was a door left ajar.

He built his argument differently after that. He stopped trying to prove that Johnson was wrong and started arguing from inside the crack, from the four dissents, from Rehnquist's grief-soaked reading of the flag's meaning. And then, in the stairwell of his own thinking, he went further: if the case was that close, then both sides had hold of something real, and his job was not to crush Trista but to press on exactly the place where the country itself was split. He wrote until one in the morning, and when he finally slept, he slept well.

Now the courtroom filled. Trista took her podium in a blazer with the sleeves pushed up, Antony sat second chair beside Anthony shuffling their notes, and Mr. Oyelaran looked over his half-glasses and said, "Counsel, you may begin whenever you're ready. This is a rehearsal, not an execution."

"Counselor," Mr. Oyelaran said, cutting in twenty minutes later, "you've told me the flag is sacred. The Court has already told us the opposite, five votes to four, in 1989. What do you want from me that five justices couldn't give the state of Texas?"

Anthony's throat went dry. He heard Trista's pen stop clicking behind him. "That it could have gone the other way," he said. "That the four dissenters in that case saw something the five didn't, or saw the same thing and weighed it differently. One vote, Your Honor. I'm not asking you to pretend the ruling doesn't exist. I'm asking you to argue as if the fifth justice had hesitated."

"Is that honest?" Mr. Oyelaran asked. It was not a hostile question. He leaned back and let it sit in the wax-smelling air.

"I don't know yet," Anthony said. "That's the part I can't get right. If I argue only from passion, I'm lying about the law. If I argue only from the law, I'm lying about the flag. My partner keeps telling me my etymology speech is tangential, and he's probably right." Antony, beside him, mouthed "I never said etymology." The judge's mouth twitched. "So I'll stand here and hold both of them, and when it stops feeling like lying, that's my argument."

Mr. Oyelaran made a note on his index card, and then another, longer one. "Recess," he said. "Ten minutes. When we come back, counsel for Johnson will respond, and I want to see if her side wobbles when yours stops shouting." He stood, gathered his cards, and went out through the door behind the bench.

In the hallway Trista bought them both pretzels from the vending machine, and they ate leaning against the marble balustrade, looking down at the lobby where a real lawyer in a wrinkled suit was arguing with a cashier about a parking validation. "Your hesitation thing," Trista said, salt on her lip. "It's better than what I've got. Mine's just recitation." She crumpled the pretzel bag in her fist. "Want to run cross-examination now, before he comes back?"

Anthony looked at the clock above the courtroom doors, at the second hand sweeping toward the ten-minute mark, and took one more bite. "Go," he said. "Hit me with your best one."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Early Decision in US college admissions is binding: a student admitted with acceptable financial aid must enroll and withdraw all other applications.
story:
The mailbox at the end of Alexia's driveway held three things on the last Saturday of October: a grocery flyer, a dental reminder, and a thin envelope from her own handwriting, returned for insufficient postage. She laughed at it, a short bitter sound, because for one half second she had thought it might be an answer, and it was only her own words coming home to her.

"Is that it?" Sean was sitting on the low wall by the sidewalk, knees apart, holding the brochure for the November 1 deadline like it was a live thing. "Is that the decision?"

"It's a returned envelope, genius. I forgot a stamp on something in like August." She folded it into her back pocket. "The decision isn't mail yet. It's barely a decision."

Sean had been arguing with her about it for two weeks, since Ms. Leblanc had posted the early application calendar on the classroom door and half the seniors had started saying the word "binding" the way people say "surgery." Alexia wanted Halloway. Halloway wanted, statistically, students who applied early. But she had done the net price calculators at midnight, alone, and the numbers moved depending on assumptions she couldn't verify, and she was sixteen with a part-time job at a garden center and a mother who said "we'll manage" in a voice that meant the opposite.

"It's binding," Sean said, for the ninth time, but this time he said it differently, slower, like he was finally hearing it. "If they take you, and the aid's okay, you have to go. You have to pull all your other applications."

"I know what binding means," Alexia said, but she didn't say it meanly, because the strange thing was that hearing it laid out plainly, there on the curb, made it newly real. She had been treating the choice like a temperament question, like introvert versus extrovert, and it wasn't. It was a rule. If they admitted her, and the aid turned out acceptable, she enrolled, and every other application died. And the part that snagged her, the part she kept circling back to, was that she would never know what the other schools would have offered, because the other offers would simply never exist. She had always thought of herself as a person who gathered options. This was a door that closed the other doors before she could even see what was behind them.

"You're going to expostulate at me," Sean said, "about how a choice made under a deadline isn't really a choice."

"I wasn't going to use that word."

"You were going to use that exact word. Sana told me you used it in English on Tuesday."

Alexia sat down on the wall beside him. The flyer fell out of the mailbox and skidded against her shoe, advertising a pumpkin sale that had already ended.

"Ms. Leblanc said something," she admitted. "Not about this. About my essay. She said the pumpkin on our porch wasn't just a pumpkin, it was synecdoche, because I'd made it stand for the whole fall, for my grandmother's kitchen, everything. And I keep thinking the deadline is like that too. Everyone treats November first as if it stands for my whole future. But it's one application. It's one envelope. It's not the whole thing, even though it feels like the whole thing."

"That's the most you've said in a week."

"I know." She pulled the returned envelope out of her pocket and looked at her own address, printed carefully in August, when the decision had been theoretical and the mailbox had just been a mailbox.

That night Sana texted her a photograph of a screenshot, no caption, just the financial aid office's page about early admits and aid appeals, and beneath it a second message: my cousin did this, applied regular everywhere, compared four offers, got way more money than the calculator said. Alexia stared at it for a long time, thumb hovering. Then she typed: but Halloway takes way fewer people regular. Then she deleted it, because that was Sean's argument, not hers, and it was extrinsic to what she actually feared. What she feared was choosing in the dark. She typed instead: can I call you in five minutes.

On the phone, Sana didn't tell her what to do. Sana said, "You keep saying Halloway is your first choice. Is it your first choice, or your first choice if the money works out, which are different things?"

"They're different things," Alexia said. "They have to be."

"Then pick which one you're actually applying with."

Alexia stood at the front window with the porch pumpkin in view, orange going soft at the stem, and understood that she had been trying to hold two ideas at once without letting them touch: that Halloway was home, and that a home you can't afford is a different place than the one you visited. She could believe both. She could also act, and acting meant choosing which belief would take the weight.

Sunday morning she walked down the driveway in her coat. She held the Halloway application in one hand and the regular decision checklist in the other, and at the mailbox she stood for a full minute, breathing fog, and then she slid the regular checklist into her bag and mailed the Halloway envelope, the one she'd had to re-stamp, its corner still creased from its first failed journey.

"Binding," she said out loud, to nobody, and dropped the little blue door of the mailbox shut with a click.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: The US Federal Reserve began raising its policy rate from near zero in March 2022 and reached a range of 5.25 to 5.50 percent in July 2023.
story:
The bank smelled like carpet cleaner and cold air, and Paige sat beside her mother at a desk near the window while a loan officer slid two offers across the blotter. Her mother read them side by side, one from 2021 that they had kept in a folder, one printed that morning. The numbers did not look like they belonged to the same country.

"Why is it so different," her mother said, not really to anyone. "Three years ago it was nearly nothing."

Paige had come along because her mother had asked her to, and because her mother still got flustered in places like this, and because she had nothing else to do on a Tuesday in July. She had not expected to care. But the gap between the two sheets bothered her the way a wrong answer bothers you before you know it is wrong, some itch of incompleteness. She took out her phone under the desk.

"Put that away," her mother murmured.

"I'm texting Krista. She did econ this year."

Krista replied fast, as she always did: ask Mr. Bennett, he's literally right there. Paige looked up. The loan officer from the next desk, the one her mother had waved at earlier like an old acquaintance, was named Mr. Bennett. He had coached something at the high school once, softball maybe, before Paige's time. He was stamping a stack of files with the absent rhythm of a man who had done it ten thousand times.

"Sir," Paige said, and her mother looked at her sharply, as if she had spoken in church. "Three years ago, when my mom got her first quote, the rate was almost zero. What changed?"

Mr. Bennett set his stamp down. "The Fed," he said. "The Federal Reserve. It started raising its policy rate in March of 2022. Near zero then. It kept going until it hit a range of 5.25 to 5.50 percent in July of last year." He picked the stamp back up. "That's about all I can tell you. The rest you'd have to ask an economist."

"It's last July?" Paige said. "Not this one."

"July 2023."

He turned back to his files, and her mother exhaled through her nose, the sound she made when she thought Paige was showing off. Paige sat with it. She remembered Krista complaining about the unit on money, the diagrams of supply and demand she had doodled over in the margins of a notebook, and she remembered her father saying at dinner once that nobody should borrow when money is expensive, though he had said it about a truck, not a mortgage, and had borrowed anyway.

At home she collated what she had: the folder of old offers, her mother's current ones, the numbers Mr. Bennett had given her, and a page Krista photographed from her econ textbook and sent with the message "this is all i got." Paige laid them out on the kitchen table in rows, oldest to newest, and read them the way she read a proof in math class, line by line, looking for the hinge. There was a version of this where it was all just weather, rates rising and falling like seasons, and a version where it was someone's decision, deliberate, with reasons behind it. She did not think those two versions canceled each other out. Somebody at the central bank had chosen to raise that rate, step after step, and the choice had traveled through the whole system until it landed on her mother's kitchen table as a monthly payment she could not make.

She wrote it out in her own words on the back of a grocery receipt. When the rate goes up, borrowing costs more, so people borrow less and spend less, so prices stop climbing so fast. She read it over and did not fully believe it. It sounded too simple, and too much like a chain of dominoes, and she knew from every experiment she had ever done in science class that causality was messier than the diagram. Maybe spending slowed for other reasons. Maybe it would have slowed anyway. She wrote underneath: not sure how much of this is the rate and how much is everything else, and left it there.

Two nights later she and Krista sat on the curb outside the Tastee Freeze, and Krista asked how the mortgage thing had gone, and Paige told her about the folder and Mr. Bennett and the receipt. "My mom thinks I made it worse," she said. "She says knowing why doesn't change the number."

"Does it?"

"I don't know yet." Paige turned her cup in her hands. "It's like geology. There's this slow metamorphic thing happening under everything, pressure that changed one rock into a different rock, and nobody at the surface feels it. Except every so often you end up sitting in a bank with your mother and there it is."

Krista laughed and said that was the most Paige sentence she had ever heard. Paige laughed too, then didn't. Across the lot her mother's car pulled in, and her mother got out slowly, folder under her arm, and stood a moment in the headlights of her own headlights before she saw them and waved.

"She's going in to sign," Paige said. "She wouldn't say which one."

She stood up and brushed the gravel off her jeans and walked toward the bank door.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: In Chicago, MLA and APA styles, entries in the final list of sources are arranged alphabetically by the author's surname, not in the order the sources were cited.
story:
Laurie told herself she had plenty of time, which was true in the sense that the paper was due Friday and it was only Tuesday, and also false in every way that mattered. She had claimed the corner table by the periodicals at the public library at four o'clock, and by six she had produced a stack of note cards, a thesis she described to herself as "basically done," and an opening paragraph she had rewritten four times without improving. She was not behind, she insisted; she was deliberating. Deliberating sounded like something scholars did.

Walker found her there because they had agreed to meet, though Laurie had half hoped he wouldn't come, since his coming would require her to show him what existed, and what existed was thinner than she wanted anyone to measure. He dropped his backpack on the chair across from her and peered at her cards. "Is that the whole Works Cited?"

"It's a draft of the whole Works Cited," Laurie said. She fanned the cards like a magician, though the trick contained nothing. She had listed her sources in the order she'd used them: first the newspaper article that had given her the idea, then two books, then a website she'd found at eleven the night before. The order told the story of her week, which felt honest to her, even intimate, like a diary of reading.

Walker picked up the cards and squinted. "You've got these in the order you cited them."

"Obviously. That's the order they happened."

"That's not how it works." He set the cards down and squared them, an annoying habit of his, as if her chaos were a tablecloth that needed straightening. "In MLA it's alphabetical by the author's last name. Same in APA, same in Chicago. Every style they showed us. Not the order you cited them."

Laurie said nothing for a moment, and in that moment she constructed, privately, an entire defense: that her system was clearer, that alphabetical order was arbitrary, that a list should reflect a mind in motion rather than a filing cabinet. She was still drafting this defense when she noticed Ms. Taylor at the reference desk, and noticed, further, that the desk itself was a rebuke. The reference books stood alphabetically. The whole library stood alphabetically. Somewhere behind her, in the stacks, thousands of authors waited in a strict and patient order that had nothing to do with who had been read first.

"I thought it was like a trail," Laurie said finally, quieter. "Like you could follow where I'd been."

"That's what footnotes are for, kind of," Walker said. "The list at the end is just a list."

It was a small correction. She wanted to impute cruelty to it, or at least condescension, to make Walker the villain of a small drama in which she was the misunderstood visionary, but the truth was he had said it the way you tell someone their shoelace is untied. She gathered the cards and began sorting them by surname, and the sorting stung more than it should have, because it revealed something else: three of her sources shared an author, and she had cited the same essay twice under two different titles, which meant she had read it twice without recognizing it, which meant her "basically done" thesis had a seam running through it that she had mistaken for a feature.

She got up and walked to the reference desk, and Ms. Taylor looked at her over her glasses in a way that suggested she had watched the whole card-sorting exchange and had opinions about it. "Is there a style manual I can look at?" Laurie asked. "MLA."

"There's one at 808," Ms. Taylor said, and then, as Laurie turned, "The one that's checked out right now is always the MLA. You'd think seniors would buy their own." This was not helpful, but it was also not aimed at Laurie, who had never imputed anything to Ms. Taylor before and did not start now, mostly because Ms. Taylor had already returned to her crossword.

The manual on the shelf, mercifully present, was spine-cracked and soft. Laurie sat on the floor between the stacks with it open in her lap, checking Walker's claim, because she did not entirely trust him either, or rather she trusted him and wanted not to. He was right. Entries in the final list went alphabetically by surname, and the little samples on the page confirmed it so plainly that she felt foolish for having argued, even silently, even to herself. In the library's hush she could hear her own earlier reasoning replay in her vernacular of self-defense, the dialect of someone who is eighteen and has been told for years that she is bright, and who has begun, nascent and clumsy at it, to distinguish between being bright and being finished.

The real problem, she saw now, was the duplicated essay, and behind it the argument itself. Her thesis claimed that city bus fares should stay flat regardless of fuel costs, a position she had arrived at from the newspaper article, but the essay she'd read twice argued the opposite, that flat fares starved the system, and she had absorbed it both times without letting it change her mind. She carried the manual back to the table and sat down across from Walker.

"I have to rewrite the middle," she said. "Not the citations. The argument. There's a guy, Okonkwo, who says flat fares broke the routes in the nineties, and I cited him like he agreed with me."

Walker blinked. "So you're switching sides?"

"No." She pulled out a clean card. "I'm saying fares should stay flat for riders and the gap should come from somewhere else, and Okonkwo is my reason for saying the somewhere else has to exist. He's not my enemy, he's my evidence." She wrote the sentence out, and it was awkward, and the second version was only slightly better, and she kept the third. She was not sure the somewhere else existed, honestly; she named a county subsidy she'd half-read about, and flagged it with a question mark, because she did not yet know if it was real and would not pretend she did.

They sorted the cards together, alphabetically, while the library's lights hummed and somewhere a printer ground through somebody else's emergency. When they finished, the list looked like everyone else's list, orderly and impersonal, and Laurie understood that it was supposed to, that the trail she'd wanted to preserve now lived where it belonged, in footnotes and in her, and not in the filing.

"Okonkwo, Reyes, Vance," Walker read off the top of the stack. "You have a source named Vance?"

"My government teacher from sophomore year wrote the newspaper article," Laurie said. "Small town."

She pulled a fresh card toward her and wrote the question mark about the subsidy on its own line, then tapped it twice against the table.

story:
The kitchen of the Rive Gauche had been a walk-in closet in some earlier life, and Mr. Mehta had filled it with a marble slab, a heat gun, and three kilos of couverture that arrived every Thursday in a box stamped with a word Tyson could not pronounce. He had taken the job for the money, mostly, but also because his mother had said a trade would steady him before college, and because there was something in the way melted chocolate moved, slow and deliberate, that made him want to be good at it.

"Tempering," Mr. Mehta said the first evening, pouring a ribbon of dark chocolate onto the slab, "is the difference between something that snaps and something that bends like an old eraser." He folded the chocolate with a scraper, working it back over itself, cooling it, warming it, watching the temperature like a hawk watches a field mouse. "You are not melting chocolate. You are convincing it."

Tyson learned the mechanics fast enough. Melt to forty-five degrees, cool to twenty-seven, bring it back up to thirty-one, hold it there. He could recite the numbers the way he'd once recited chemistry valences, and by the third week he could do the whole sequence without checking the thermometer twice. But his chocolates came out of the fridge dull, and on the fourth week they came out worse: a pale, gritty film across the tops, like frost on a window that someone had rubbed with sand.

He set one of the spoiled pieces on the counter and stared at it while the dishwashers clattered behind him. His phone buzzed. Aden, texting from the library: did u get the job at the fancy place. Tyson typed back: yes. tempering chocolate. its going bad tho, white powdery stuff on top. Aden replied within a minute, and the message was longer than anything Aden usually sent, because Aden wanted this, wanted Tyson to succeed at the kitchen, wanted it so badly he'd been talking about it to everyone at school since Tyson got hired.

dont panic, Aden wrote. my grandma makes chocolate in her shop back home and this happened to her once. she said its called sugar bloom. its a dry gritty white coating, the humidity thing. moisture dissolves sugar on the surface and it recrystallizes when it dries. she said stop putting them in the cold fridge and then dragging them out into this humid air, the condensation ruins them. store them cool and dry instead. Tyson read the message twice, then held one of the chocolates under the light and rubbed the film with his fingertip. Dry. Gritty. Not greasy like the butterfat problem Mr. Mehta had shown him, but sandy, crystalline, exactly what Aden's grandmother had described. His tempering had probably been fine all week. He had been sabotaging the finished pieces himself, chilling them hard and then carrying the trays out through the steam of the dish pit, where the humid air met the cold chocolate and left its condensation behind.

He thought about it while he scraped the marble clean. At school, in the abstract, he liked problems that could be operationalized: define the variable, isolate it, test. Mr. Mehta's way of thinking was different, older, a kind of attention that didn't reduce things to variables at all. He watched chocolate the way you might watch weather coming across a steppe, patient and unhurried, reading the whole sky instead of one instrument. Tyson had assumed the dull chocolates meant his numbers were wrong. It hadn't occurred to him that the failure could happen after the numbers, in the space between the fridge and the shelf, in the ordinary damp air of a working kitchen. Both ways of seeing were true, he decided. The thermometer told him part of it, and the watching told him the rest, and he would need both, though he still wasn't sure which one to trust first.

He made a new batch that afternoon, tempering carefully, and this time he let the molds set in the dry storage room near the office, where the air conditioner ran but nothing steamed. Malaika came in at four to prep the evening's dessert station and found him crouched in front of the storage shelf with a penlight, examining each piece like a jeweler.

"Are those for the tasting menu?" she said. "Because Chef asked me to plate six of them tonight and if they look like that again he's going to take us both off the station." She wanted that station; she'd told Tyson she was saving for culinary school and the plating work was the one line on her application she couldn't write herself. She picked up a piece and turned it in the light. It shone, dark and glassy, the way Mr. Mehta's did.

"Snap it," Tyson said. She did, and it broke clean, with the sound of a small dry branch. She held the two halves up like evidence.

"Okay," she said. "Okay. What did you fix?"

"Not the chocolate," Tyson said. "The room I put it in. Long story. There's a text on my phone you can read." He gathered six perfect pieces onto a white plate, the penlight still in his pocket, and carried them out toward the pass where the first orders of the evening were already hanging, the printer chattering, and Mr. Mehta looked up from the stove and said, "Finally."
